Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there is considerable misapprehension as far as the cherry situation, which was mentioned here, is concerned. My information is that a thousand tons of cherries which growers were unable to market were put into frozen form at their own cost, and they are holding them at the present time rather than a thousand tons having been left on the trees to rot. Various proposals were considered which the growers' representatives wished to discuss with their organization. The two groups-the Ontario peach growers' marketing board and the processors-have requested a further meeting with the stabilization board on Thursday.
In other words, during the past week there have been a series of meetings and negotiations going on with the stabilization board, the peach producers' marketing board and the canners, in which I might say the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Smith) has been taking a very active part.

Broadcasting

The house resumed, from Monday, August 25, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-55, to establish a board of broadcast governors and to provide for the continuance of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation- Mr. Nowlan-Mr. Sevigny in the chair.
On clause 5-Chairman chief executive officer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose last night, we were considering clause 5 of this bill. Shall clause 5 carry?

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Salaries and fees.

Clause 6, Mr. Chairman, deals with the remuneration of the members of the proposed board. It is quite obvious from this clause that the board is going to be a considerable cost to the taxpayers, and that the remuneration of the members of this board will be considerably in excess of that which the board members of the corporation now receive. I believe I am right in saying that under the present legislation governing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or regulations made under that legislation, there is a ceiling on the remuneration of the executive committee of the C.B.C. of $1,000; that other members of the board of the present corporation receive $50 per meeting and expenses while they are in Ottawa, and there is a ceiling on their remuneration of $500.
The minister will probably recall that the Fowler commission recommended that remuneration of the members of the proposed board should not exceed $30,000 per annum exclusive of travelling expenses. But no such limitation, as we had on the remuneration of the members of the previous board has been included in this bill. I should think, Mr. Chairman, in view of that fact and that the remuneration of members of this proposed board has been doubled, the cost to the taxpayers might be at least $100,000 per year or even a good deal more than that.
I was wondering whether the minister or the Minister of Finance had made any estimate of the annual cost of this proposed board. It seems to me this is a very important item, as the board will be holding public meetings, which in some cases would be protracted, and extend over many days, and would be very expensive. Has the minister given any consideration to this, and could he indicate why the remuneration of the members of this board has been doubled
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
without any limit having been imposed on it, as was done under the previous act?

In so far as the part-time members are concerned, the remuneration was doubled because we were advised by officers of the corporation that from their experience it was very difficult to get former members, except at great sacrifice, to come to the meetings. There was increasing difficulty during the last few years because of rising costs and so on, and members came at a real sacrifice. It was not fair to expect that to continue, and in fact some change would have been made in the remuneration payable to members of the old board if that had continued.
In so far as the ceiling itself is concerned, the Leader of the Opposition appreciates that we differed from the Fowler report, as he pointed out yesterday. We now have three full-time members who will be paid a salary fixed by the governor in council. I can say no consideration has been given to the amount which should be paid. We anticipate that we shall have to pay substantial amounts to attract the men who will be asked to fill these positions. Hence I am not in a position to give an estimate of the overall expenditure which will be made.

The minister's last observation, namely that no consideration has yet been given to the salaries that will be paid these gentlemen, raises a point in my mind. This board is to have a judicial character. It has always been a well understood principle of our constitution that the salary of judges is fixed by parliament and is never left in any way under the control of the executive. It seems to me that this is another way in which-again I am not insinuating that it would be done-it would be possible to bring pressure to bear in certain cases. It seems to me that it should be a statutory provision and not a provision made by the governor in council. I would ask the minister whether he would not consider allowing this particular clause to stand and with his colleagues give some consideration to that point.

I am prepared to give consideration to all the suggestions which are made, Mr. Chairman. As I said, this bill is not finality in itself. It will be changed from time to time. But I would point out to the hon. member that the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. is paid such salary as the governor in council may determine and that the legislation which is now before us provides that the chairman of the new board shall be paid such annual salary as the governor in council shall determine.
Quite so.
There is therefore no change at all in the bill.

No; but the minister will recall that what he was asserting as a great virtue of this new set-up was that it was going to be judicial, that it was going to replace the former situation where it was alleged that one competitor had jurisdiction over another. It seems to me that if, in fact, we take seriously this judicial aspect, we should follow the practice which has always been accepted, namely that any body having judicial functions should have the maximum independence that it is possible for parliament to give it. I wonder whether the minister would not allow this item to stand until after lunch, when he could have a chance to discuss it with some of his colleagues.

I am in the hands of the committee, Mr. Chairman. But as far as my colleagues are concerned, may I say that we have discussed this matter and we have deliberately left it open until we had an opportunity to see how the board operates, and also what will have to be done with regard to attracting the type of people here that we want and expect. I agree with everything the hon. member says about a judicial body, but may I point out to him that the pension commission is a judicial body, and the government of which he was a member changed the salaries of the members and chairman of that board, despite the fact that it was fixed; and it was done by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are also other examples.

Yes, but I would recall to my hon. friend's mind that we did it over the very strenuous objections of the opposition. I think it was done before I was a member of the government, but I remember the debates very well. The most violent objections were taken by many hon. members on the other side of the house on precisely the ground that I am suggesting here. I might also point out that although the pension commission does have a semi-judicial function in some respects, at any rate, it is not the kind of body on which there would really be any suspicion that any government might wish to exert any kind of pressure. The government never appears before it as a litigant, as it does before the courts. The government would have no motive that is very easily discernible for seeking by this indirect means to bring pressure to bear on that commission.
Broadcasting
But I suggest that this is precisely what we on this side of the house are most concerned about, and what I understood the minister to say on behalf of the government they were most concerned about, namely to make this body highly judicial in its character. It seemed to me that to remove any suspicion that the government was using the remuneration to bring pressure on the board, it would be better for parliament to set the remuneration.

All we are doing is trying to give the government an opportunity to follow the course which they so strongly advocated when they were on this side with respect to a body the judicial character of v/hich they have continually emphasized.

I have pointed out that in the case of 12 of the 15 members the remuneration is fixed by the statute before us. The remuneration of the other three members is not fixed, and cannot be fixed at the moment because of the reasons I have mentioned. The government has to take responsibility for the choice of these men, and I can assure the committee that this government-and I think any other government, as far as that is concerned-is not going to exercise pressure on the men chosen for this board through any alteration whatsoever in the inducement respecting salaries.
This is another example of those things which would have been dealt with by the committee if the bill had been introduced in time to enable that to be done.
No, because the bill would have stood the way it is.
Will the three members have the same salary scale, or will there be a higher salary for the chairman, a lower salary for the vice-chairman, and so on?
No decision has been made on that point. Possibly the chairman will be paid a little more.
I wonder if the minister can assure the committee that once the salary has been fixed by order in council there will be no move to modify that salary during their term of office.

I certainly can give no such assurance. It would only be in an unusual situation that that would have to be done, but I can imagine a situation where a person has been appointed and performs very valuable service, and is then given an opportunity to enter some other field at a much higher rate of salary. In such a situation it is possible that the government might consider increasing the salary to keep that incumbent

Broadcasting
there. Again, the term of office is seven years, and the holder might be reappointed for a further seven years. That is a long time, and I should not care to give such a commitment as has been suggested. I do not think any responsible minister could.
I only had in mind a reduction in salary being made.
I do not think there will be a reduction.

I see there are three full-time members, and that in order to sit the board will need a quorum of five. Thus they will have to ask at least two of the part-time members to sit with them, and the remuneration paid to them is $100 a day. As it is now, the board may sit every day, month after month, and in this way part-time members may become more highly paid than those who are full-time members. Has this point been considered by the cabinet?
No; consideration has not been given to that.

That is a very important
point, because one of the purposes of this board would be to hold hearings, and these hearings might be prolonged. At $100 a day plus expenses it would not be hard for part time members to reach a salary of $15,000 or $20,000. Surely that is an argument for placing a maximum on the remuneration of part-time members, as was done in the case of the C.B.C.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 7-Staff.

I notice that the staff of the board are to be appointed under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. I would imagine that certain of the functions of the board of broadcast governors are now being performed by certain of the staff of the C.B.C. who are not civil servants under the Civil Service Act.
I have no objection whatsoever to any new employees being appointed under the provisions of that act, but I wonder if there is any provision made for the incorporation of such employees as I have mentioned, or whether any consideration has been given to that point; because I am sure the minister does not intend to terminate the employment of people who would have no function under the reorganized C.B.C. but who, because of their experience, might I think be invaluable to the new board. I think it would be very unfortunate if persons who had been employed for a very long time should be made subject to competitive examination.

I recognize, of course, that the governor in council under the Civil Service Act has authority to appoint civil servants and to dispense with certain normal requirements of the Civil Service Act, but I should not have thought the minister would wish to proceed in that way, and I wonder whether some other provision should not be made in respect of such persons as I have mentioned.

The problem of transferring individuals who, perhaps, are older and who may not wish to take examinations which could be prejudicial to them is something which will have to be dealt with. As the hon. member has said, there is provision for exemption from this requirement, and I imagine this mechanism will be used. Then if the hon. gentleman will turn to clause 41 of the bill he will see that provision is made there preserving the rights of all the employees of the C.B.C. who are under the public service act; and the intention is, if and when these employees are transferred to the civil service, by examination or by exemption or whatever method is used, that their rights will be preserved. I can assure the hon. gentleman that there will be no trouble whatsoever in dealing with this situation.
Can the minister give us an assurance that there is no intention whatsoever to use this as an indirect means of getting rid of some employees?
If the government should decide to get rid of some employees it would not have to use indirect means; it would use direct means.

In connection with the staff situation, I wonder if the minister has any idea of the number of staff now with the C.B.C. who would be transferred to the new board in order to make its work more effective. I am thinking particularly of audience research work, which might be very useful to the board of broadcast governors. Or there might be a possibility that the present audience research group now with the C.B.C. could do work for the board of governors on request. There is also the question of the regulation group which the C.B.C. now has in existence. Is it planned to transfer this group to the control of the board of broadcast governors?

The regulatory duties now performed by the C.B.C. would be turned over to the new board, and I should think some of that staff-I am not sure of the exact division-would naturally be used by the board of broadcast governors whenever possible.

In so far as the great majority of the employees are concerned, they are of course engaged in the operating end. We have under the C.B.C. directly over 6,000 employees at the moment, and only a very small proportion of these are engaged in the regulatory work or in the program research work to which the hon. member has referred. The great majority would be staying with the C.B.C., under the control of that corporation.

There is another question which occurs to me. The quasi-judicial functions which will be performed by this board will obviously require it to have almost constant and continuous legal advice. Is it intended that the Department of Justice should provide legal advisers to the board in the way it does to government departments, or is it intended that the board should have a legal department of its own?

That is a matter which I think will have to be left to be decided in the light of experience and the judgment of the board. No decision has yet been made, and until a decision is reached, or a change is made, the officers of the Department of Justice are being used by the government and will be used, initially at least, by the board.

I wonder if the minister has made an estimate with respect to the staff, regardless of where it will be recruited, from the standpoint of the cost to the country of this new set-up. Of course the money will have to be voted. Can the minister give the committee an estimate of what that is likely to cost?

At the moment I am not in a position to give that estimate, Mr. Chairman. We are starting here afresh with a completely new organization. One could take the salaries and wages paid in the C.B.C. to those engaged in regulation, I suppose, and get a rough estimate, but it could only be a rough one. I would prefer not to venture a figure. We will have the responsibility of providing estimates for this body at the next session. At that time the board will be appointed. The board will make a survey and estimate what staff is required, and then we will be able to give an estimate that is an accurate appreciation of the problem for the first year, but at this stage I am not in a position to do that.

It is rather difficult to reach conclusions and decisions because the minister is asking parliament to give him a blank cheque, so to speak, to carry out this project. I believe it would have been advisable for
Broadcasting
the committee to be given some idea as to what this new venture is likely to cost the country.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 8 agreed to.
On clause 9-Executive committee.

Mr. Chairman, clause 9 is a very important clause of this bill. It deals with the executive committee which, as I said last evening, will be the committee responsible, I would think, for the day to day work of this board. Three of its members will be the full-time members of the board. While I agree that in this clause the powers of the executive committee are limited in certain respects, and quite rightly so, and that this limitation will prevent it from promulgating regulations which would have to be passed by the full board in dealing with certain important matters, nevertheless the executive committee would, I assume, have the power to interpret regulations passed by the full board. That perhaps will be just as important in a body of this kind as the regulations themselves.
I take it that under this clause the executive committee can also draft proposals and regulations for consideration by the board. That is why I want to emphasize the importance of this smaller group, especially the three full-time members within it. Subclause 3 of clause 9, which as I said limits the powers of the executive committee, reads as follows:
(3) The executive committee shall exercise such of the powers and functions of the board as are delegated to it by the board, except the powers and functions of the board under sections 11 and 12 and the provisions of section 13 other than paragraph (b) of subsection (4) thereof.
Excluded from that limitation is paragraph (b) of subsection 4 of section 13. I wonder if the minister could explain why that exception was made.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. When hon. gentlemen look at paragraph (b) they will see it provides power to grant or revoke permission to a licensee to operate the broadcasting station in respect of which his licence was issued as part of any network for the broadcasting of a particular program or a series of programs extending over a period not exceeding one month. In other words there will have to be two different decisions made. Perhaps arrangements will be made for establishing a network for a hockey game, or perhaps a temporary network will be established for a series of hockey or football games over a period not exceeding one month. That is the type of network you could safely leave to a small executive committee without any suggestion of impropriety, and it would

Broadcasting
be most unfortunate if some of these things were delayed because you could not get the executive or the whole board together to provide for them.
We had an embarrassing situation with respect to the football game last Saturday night, as hon. members know. After a great deal of delay and changes made in network programs the game was telecast and the reception was terrible; you could not see it.
What was wrong?

Clause agreed to.
On clause 10-Objects and purposes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would not do well to explain exactly what are the objects and purposes of this clause. I have in mind now particularly the latter part of this clause, which states:
The board shall . . . regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting
stations-
-and so on. What is meant by "regulation" and what is meant by "operation"? Those are the two questions I would direct to the minister now, leaving two others for later consideration.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest this simply means that the board shall regulate pursuant to clause 11, which gives it the power to make regulations. In other words the board shall have the power to establish regulations for the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations which, as the hon. member knows, is a phrase borrowed almost word for word from the existing act under which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation operates.
Clause 10 is not an operative clause. As the hon. member will appreciate, this is a general statement of powers and objects. They are defined and set forth in the following clauses, Nos. 11, 12 and 13. I believe hon. gentlemen will find that everything in clause 10 would be generally subject to the specific powers set forth in those clauses.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do I take it, then, that the regulation and operation will be in the same manner as carried on heretofore?
That will be a decision the new board will have to make.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Dealing with the latter part of clause 10, which states that the board shall regulate the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them, could the minister indicate to the committee in what way the regulation of those activities is going to be
	.	-
conducted in so far as (a) the C.B.C. itself is concerned and (b) private broadcasting stations are concerned?

Mr. Chairman, I am not certain that I follow the hon. member of fully understand the meaning of his question. The regulations, of course, will be generally for both private stations and the corporation as is spelled out in the act. In future the corporation will have to appear before the board if it wants a licence for a new station and be treated in the same way as any other person in that field. That wording is put there specifically to show that this board is going to have general supervision over all broadcasting in Canada, which I take it is the intention and design of this government. As I said yesterday, this is a provision that is eminently desirable so as to avoid any criticism of the C.B.C. in future for being in an invidious position vis-a-vis the private broadcasting stations. We have tried to rectify that, and that is why we have spelled out here "over private and public stations".

Mr. Chairman, I believe this clause of the bill which spells out the general purposes of the board is the most controversial clause in the bill, because it really does not give us too much to put our teeth into. The bulk of the purpose is contained in a long clause that is stuck in the middle of the paragraph. Because we feel it is not sufficiently definite, at this time I move seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia:
That this clause be struck out in its entirety and the following substituted:
The board is charged with the supervision, regulation, and control of all broadcasting in Canada in the public interest. The board is to ensure the provision of a varied and comprehensiye broadcasting service, on a national basis and with a high standard and a basically Canadian content and character; and it is to examine the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and to determine the relationship between the private and public stations.
As the minister will note, there are not too many changes from the present clause 10 except to take the first sentence from the draft act of the Fowler commission and put it in here, and then to emphasize the power of the board of broadcast governors to regulate completely, or control completely, the relationship between the public and private stations. We think this amendment will help assure those of us who are concerned about the possibility of the board of broadcast governors not carrying out the intent of this legislation in the public interest, perhaps leading to the withering away of the public broadcasting system we have. We would be much encouraged if this particular clause, which we have suggested as

an amendment, were accepted in place of the one that is now in the bill.

Mr. Chairman, in so far as the intention expressed by the hon. member is concerned, I could have no quarrel with that whatsoever, and I think generally there is intent not to materially alter the section, perhaps, but to emphasize certain features of it. I must point out, Mr. Chairman, that this section, as was the case with all other sections but particularly with this one, engaged the attention of the chief draftsman of the Department of Justice, and a great deal of careful consideration was given to it in view of the legal questions generally involved.
I would not want to take, and I cannot take, the responsibility of accepting an amendment such as this without further consideration and without experience of operation. I think the intention is all right, but I would point out for instance that in the draft amendment which I have in my hand, which the hon. gentleman has just moved, hon. members will see that the board is charged with supervision, regulation and control of all broadcasting in Canada in the public interest. We have deliberately included in the first line or two of section 10 the words:
The board shall, for the purpose of ensuring the continued existence and efficient operation of a national broadcasting system-
We wanted to make it clear that we were going to continue something. Maybe there is not a material difference between the two, but we have given some importance to that point so as to see that the existing corporation and everything else are to be continued and operated. Then again, there is another clause which could be very important, because the last line but one of section 10 of the bill before us says:
-and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
That also does not appear in the draft amendment which was submitted to us. It is true that provisions for appeal except on questions of law are excluded from the bill; but all lawyers know

everyone knows-that there are means which can be taken such as certiorari or mandamus, or something of that kind, if members of the board are involved in legal matters. These words "final determination" were deliberately included in the section so that this board of broadcast governors would be able to make adjudication without having to worry too much about technical matters of a purely delaying nature which may arise.
Provision for appeal to the courts is safeguarded, as I said, on questions of law. For
57071-3-260
Broadcasting
these reasons, and because primarily the section was, as I said, considered very carefully by the justice department draftsmen, I cannot accept the amendment moved by the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks I wished to make on section 10 and the point of view I had wished to put forward are very well embodied in the wording of this amendment which we are happy to support.
Section 10 is, I think the minister will agree, perhaps the most important section in the whole bill, and all the more important because it declares certain objects and purposes of this legislation which override anything which appears in part II of the bill dealing with the C.B.C. Indeed, I think section 29, subsection 2 of part II specifically provides that the corporation is bound by the provisions of part I. Therefore everything in part II is subject to part I and would be subject to section 10, which declares the objects and purposes of this board.
While I am quite willing to accept the statement of the minister as to these objects and purposes however they may be expressed in this section and as he has indicated in his statement, I do think it would be advisable to strengthen the language of this section, as is done in this amendment, to emphasize the importance of a national broadcasting system conducted as a public service in the public interest; something that has been emphasized by everyone concerned with this matter from Sir John Aird and Right Hon. R. B. Bennett on down. Indeed, it is also emphasized on more than one occasion in the reports of the Massey commission and the Fowler commission. But section 10, though it may be implicit, is silent in respect of that particular emphasis.
I should perhaps take advantage of this opportunity to apologize to the minister for a statement I made last night which was quite inaccurate. I think I said in one of my interventions that there was no reference to a national broadcasting system in section 10. Of course there is a reference to it, and I am sorry I was inaccurate in that sense; but reference to the national broadcasting system is not in the emphatic terms that I think it should be.
The minister has indicated that the language used here was chosen deliberately to emphasize the continued existence of a national system; but if he goes back to the C.B.C. legislation he will find that the language used there-and I will come back to the language in another section of the report-charges the C.B.C. with continuing a national broadcasting system in the public interest. It puts a definite obligation on the C.B.C. to do that

Broadcasting
in stronger terms than I suggest are used in section 10 in relation to this new board.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, we think this amendment should be supported. I believe it realizes some of the objectives that we have in mind; it strengthens those objectives, and I think would make this a better bill in the public interest, improving the public service character of broadcasting.

I would like to say a word or two in support of the amendment. My method of supporting it is to examine very carefully the present clause, because it seems to me if you read the present clause without the phrase to which the minister referred, if you read the operative part of it, you will find that the board has the power to regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters, and so on. It will be seen there that all the powers the board is given are the powers to regulate; there are no powers to initiate.
Now, it is true it is said here that the board must have this purpose in mind under those regulations; but what the Fowler commission recommended and what the hon. member for Port Arthur has, I think, imported into his amendment is the power to initiate, and that is precisely what we think there ought to be. It is not good enough just to be able to regulate. It seems to me the whole concept of this clause is too negative, and for that reason it would be far better to put something in it that would be a direction, which as the Leader of the Opposition has said exists in the C.B.C. legislation now on the statute books, to initiate, that is to be the fountainhead, the inspiration of broadcasting activities, both public and private.

Mr. Chairman, I find some difficulty in reconciling clause 10 as it appears in the bill with the statements of the minister. My difficulty in that respect is added to by the minister's statement a moment ago that he found no quarrel with the intention expressed by the mover of the amendment. I should like to take clause 10 and see if I can get some help from the minister on it. I want to read it and isolate certain words in doing so. It reads as follows. The board shall-
-for the purpose of ensuring the continued existence and efficient operation of a national broadcasting system and the provision of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service of a high standard that is basically Canadian in content and character-
If you take that group of words you can see that they might well have been put in the preamble to the bill. They are a separate

statement of purpose, and probably should be in the preamble. One can express different points of view about them.

They would not be
effective if they were in the preamble.

That is the point I am
making. The Prime Minister has interjected that they are not effective here.
If they were in the preamble they would not be effective.

One might say that they contain a pious hope somewhat badly expressed. We all, of course, want a basically Canadian content and character; that is the purpose of the whole thing. We all want the continued existence of the national broadcasting system, its efficient operation and so on. The point I am getting at is that this group of words deals separately with one aspect of the matter, whether they are in a separate clause or in this one; but leaving these words aside, and I respectfully submit that is the way the clause must be read if we are to get its legal meaning, the operative part of the clause reads as follows. The board shall-
.-regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
It will be seen that there are five separate matters dealt with in this one clause, and for some strange reason they are all grouped together in this rather unusual form. The first one I dealt with, embodying a laudable statement of objectives, might well be in the preamble; but the effective and operative ones are, first, that the board shall regulate the establishment and operation of networks. That is fairly clear. Second, the board shall regulate the activities of public and private stations. I want to draw the attention of the minister to that point particularly. That means all individual stations. It is perhaps clear enough with respect to the privately owned stations, but in the case of the C.B.C. it means that the board can regulate the activities of an individual station in the network operated by the C.B.C. From anything said by the minister I do not think that was intended. I do not think that is the purpose of the bill.
Third, the board can regulate the relationship between individual stations, so the board can regulate the relationship between two individual stations operated by the publicly owned organization, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There has been no suggestion that this is what was intended.

Then there is the other provision to which the minister referred a minute ago. In the fourth place it should be noted that the board can provide, not regulate, for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto. I take it that "in relation thereto" relates to any of the matters previously mentioned. Therefore the board can provide for the final determination of all matters in relation to individual stations.
That is the point that is causing me concern. I think I intimated last night that I understood the minister's objectives and what he was seeking to do, but I find myself in great difficulty in dealing with this clause. Notwithstanding what the minister said about the draftmanship of clause 10, I respectfully submit that it does not do the things that he has expressed himself as wishing to do. Indeed, it causes considerable alarm because the board is given the power to meddle in detailed matters concerning individual stations. That is the point I wish to make and which is concerning me. If it does that, then it comes immediately and directly into conflict with the C.B.C. which is operating the publicly owned stations. It is not the part about regulating networks that is bothering me at all, but rather the power to interfere in matters concerning individual stations as such. I should like to have the minister's comment on that point.

I am tempted to rise, Mr. Chairman, because in looking at the minister I have come to the conclusion that he is almost persuaded. I wish to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur and his explanation in regard thereto. I am not going to repeat what he said. We fully realize that if the amendment is accepted by the minister, and I see us getting closer to our objective as the minutes go by, there will have to be one or two other amendments in part II to give effect to this amendment, but we can deal with them later provided we can persuade the minister that this amendment is necessary.
In that connection I want to read one paragraph from a press release issued yesterday by the Canadian broadcasting league. The minister knows that this organization is composed of people who have taken a very serious interest in Canadian broadcasting policy over a long period of time. This is what they have to say:
The Canadian broadcasting league has carefully considered the new broadcasting bill. The league welcomes the government's statements on the intention of the new legislation. It welcomes also the fact that the bill preserves the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and appears to provide for a single national broadcasting system under the control of a large representative board of broadcast governors. The league believes, however, the
57071-3-260J
Broadcasting
bill should make this principle absolutely clear by two additional provisions: First, the board of broadcast governors should be explicitly charged with the duty of reporting on the whole of broadcasting in Canada, public and private. Second, the C.B.C., as part of the single national system, should report to the board of broadcast governors. We hope these points will be cleared up during the debate.
I am not going to take any more time. I wanted to bring that paragraph to the attention of the minister and the committee. In view of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur and the proposals made by members of the official opposition I would urge the minister to give further consideration to the amendment of this clause to give effect to the wishes of those who are seriously concerned with making certain that the minister attains his own objectives with respect to the purposes of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister is letting a number of questions accumulate and will answer them together. I am concerned about the phrase in line 20, "for the final determination of all matters"! I draw the minister's attention to the fact that clause 10, consisting of about 9 lines, is all one sentence. It is an unusually long sentence, and I have some apprehension when that long sentence is wound up with the words that the board shall "provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto".
I wonder whether the minister, who is a well known solicitor, thinks that under this clause, if there is dissatisfaction it might be difficult for that person to refer the matter, as is the inherent right of everyone, to the courts. Does he not think those words "for final determination of all matters" would be difficult to overcome unless some provision is made to allow any citizen who is displeased with any part whatever of that long sentence to have full recourse to the courts?

The general intention indicated by all those who have spoken in favour of this amendment, Mr. Chairman, is in agreement with the attitude of the government. There is no question whatever but that it is intended to operate this board and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the public interest, and that surely does not have to be spelled out. It is implicit in every section of the bill and in everything I and the other members of the government have said on this bill.
As I said earlier, I am not prepared to accept the responsibility for changing the clause at this time, a clause on which a good deal of time was spent by a very, shall we say, careful draftsman. I could go further than that, as the hon. member for Ottawa West well knows. The government cannot accept

Broadcasting
this amendment, although it certainly accepts the intention implicit in it.
In so far as the hon. member for Ottawa West analysed the clause, I am inclined to accept his analysis, at any rate the first part. In so far as objects and powers are concerned, I am not sure where objects leave off and powers begin. This is a general statement. I would not want to go as far as he did in his description of it, and he could not expect me to accept that. However, this is a general statement of intention. I cannot accept at all the statement of the Leader of the Opposition that it is purely negative, because after all you have to read this general statement with the powers set forth in clauses 11, 12 and 13. There is certainly nothing negative in those. There are powers to initiate and all sorts of powers. When you spell out those powers and take them in addition to clause 10, I think you will have everything this committee requires in so far as protective measures are concerned.
As I said yesterday, and as is axiomatic, it does not make very much difference what words you have in these clauses so long as you have personnel appointed who are going to see that the measure is administered in accordance with the intentions. If they are going to administer this in the national interest, then the public is going to be protected. You can have all the safeguarding sections in the world, but if you have administrators who take a careless attitude it will not do any good. I believe, and the government believes, that this clause 10 does spell out, in general terms followed by succeeding clauses, that broadcasting will be in the national interests of Canada. We have to ask the committee to accept clause 10 as it is presently drafted.

The last question I raised related to the fifth power given to the board under this clause, that the board shall provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto. Bearing in mind that the board can deal with individual stations, I wonder if the minister would address himself to that point; because as I see it, the board is given the power to go into activities and the determination of questions in relation to individual stations. That would be directly in conflict with matters which would be regarded as normal and proper activities of the C.B.C. I wonder if the minister would address himself to just that aspect of the matter.

It may be that these words are capable of the wide interpretation the hon. member has given them, but it is certainly not the intention of the government. I point out to him, as he undoubtedly

knows, that when he speaks of a network operated by the C.B.C. you have first the publicly owned stations, which are owned by the C.B.C., and then you have various classes of affiliates, some who asked to be affiliated and some who have been ordered, shall we say, to be affiliated. There are various categories there, the details of which I have not got but which I will have when we come to the second section of the bill.
Reverting to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Ottawa West, I may say I thought it was improper to have the officers of the C.B.C. sitting in front of me to deal with this part of the bill so far as the board of broadcast governors is concerned because they are strangers, so to speak, to it. So far as the C.B.C. is concerned, when we come to the second part dealing with it, then with the committee's consent I intend to have officers of the C.B.C. here so that any questions dealing with the corporation can be answered at that time. If there is the implication that the hon. member reads into that section, it is because of the various classes of stations which are affiliated with the C.B.C. The hon. member will also notice that the board has the power, at the request of a station and after a public hearing of which the C.B.C. has been given notice, to permit the station to withdraw from that affiliation.
Perhaps I could clarify my point for the minister. My concern was not with this power as it concerns networks or groups of stations, but as it concerns individual stations. That was my concern.

There are individual stations within a network, and various categories of stations. A subsequent clause gives them the right, if they wish, to withdraw. There has to be some control over these stations.

Incidentally, may I mention a small matter. I do not think I used the word "negative" in my description of this paragraph at all. Someone else may have done so. The clause says that the board shall regulate the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them. I do not know whether or not this point was brought up in the previous discussion, but my non-legal mind was not able to follow all its ramifications. Does this clause mean that the board shall regulate the relationship between separate private broadcasting stations and not merely the relationships between private and public stations, that is the relationship between stations within each category?

I think the intention is to regulate public and private stations and their relationship to each other. I do not believe

the board would, except in so far as there was an infringement or a matter affecting a particular regulation, act as a judge or adjudicator on matters affecting two private stations, unless it came within the scope of the next three sections.
While I appreciate the attention which has been given to clause 10, because it is a general statement, frankly I think most lawyers in this house would agree privately that clause 10 is not operative except as it is interpreted by the three succeeding clauses, which in my opinion are the heart of the bill from an operative standpoint.
The minister is satisfied that the language in clause 10 could not be used for the purpose of regulation as between separate private stations?

I wonder if the minister is quite sure about that, because an example of one kind of situation which does arise between private stations has been drawn to the minister's attention, I believe, in this house. This case concerned stations, somewhat remote geographically from one another, which had almost the same wave length, and this resulted in a real conflict between the private stations. I would apprehend that the board would have power to deal with that; or would it come within the purview of the Department of Transport?

Without any question I would think that would come within the purview of the board. As I explained to the Leader of the Opposition, I was very careful to say "subject to the specific powers set forth in the next three sections". Anything which arises in the following sections generally-I will not say "anything" but generally- would come within the purview of the board for adjudication. All these matters, I would think, would be dealt with generally by the board.

Bearing in mind the minister's answer to the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Chairman, if you look at line 18 you find this language. The board shall-
-regulate . . . the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them.
He will note that from the way in which it is now drafted, "between them" relates to "stations". If he wanted to do what he just expressed to the Leader of the Opposition, should he not repeat the words "broadcasting stations" after the word "public" and before the word "and" in line 18, so it would read:
The board shall . . . regulate . . . the activities of public broadcasting stations and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them.
Broadcasting
"Between them" would obviously then relate to the two groups of stations as opposed to the individual. That was one of the difficulties that concerned us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Port Arthur moves-

Before the question is put to the committee, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask a question of the minister. Is this clause 10 to be prepared just for those who have legal training? It is hard to understand for one who has not such training. In my opinion the amendment seems to be easier to understand for those who have not legal training. The discussion between the hon. member for Ottawa West and the minister, both of whom are good lawyers, seems to be comprehensible; but when we come to read it, those who have not the training do not seem to understand this clause 10 as clearly as we understand the amendment which appears to accomplish the same purpose.
This is why I do not understand why the amendment was not accepted. It does not seem to have any very important change in it, but it seems to be much clearer for the balance of the people in Canada when they come to read it.
Question.

I accept the statement that the intention is the same, either with respect to the other amendments or the one that is now before us, except that the clause provides for final determination and also provides what I think is more important for ensuring the continued existence of the system. The difference between them may not be so very great. The hon. member for Hull says this is a legal argument. The hon. member for Ottawa West refers to this as a sort of platitude. I therefore do not think that perhaps legal questions are so much involved in any event.
In any case, I stand on the explanation I gave at the beginning. This is a section which has been very carefully drafted and has been reviewed over and over again by the draftsman. I am not prepared to take responsibility myself for accepting an amendment to it, even though I think the amendment is of the same tenor and the same spirit. Nevertheless the legal implications, as the hon. member for Ottawa West and others know, can be different. We therefore must ask the committee to accept the section as it is now before it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The question is as follows: The hon. member for Port Arthur moves:
That clause 10 be struck out in its entirety and the following substituted:
The hoard is charged with the supervision, regulation and control of all broadcasting in Canada in the public interest. The board is to ensure the provision of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service, on a national basis and with a high standard and a basically Canadian content and character; and it is to examine the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and to determine the relationship between the private and public stations.
Before I put the question I should inform the committee that it is the opinion of the Chair that the proposed amendment is irregular in this sense, that you cannot delete a clause by means of an amendment. This clause should be negatived before inserting a new one. In support of this proposition I believe that Beauchesne should be read, citations 402, 404 and 408. In clause 402, subparagraph (1) we find the following:
(1) In committee all the clauses of the bill are considered before any new clauses are brought up and added to the bill. But this practice is not rigorously followed and the committee is generally guided by what is most convenient in each particular case.
In this particular case I believe that for the sake of expediency the question should be put to the committee.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 28; nays, 86.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 11-Regulations.

Mr. Chairman, we shall have some specific proposals with regard to the subsection and perhaps some amendments. However, there are one or two general observations on the whole section that I should like to make to the minister, and perhaps he will be able to enlighten me on one or two of the points I am going to raise.
This section, with the following section 12, I take it is the one which will implement section 10 which has relation to the objects and purposes of the bill. As I understand it-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-this section, indeed the bill itself, does not provide-as have all previous broadcasting bills and as various commissions dealing with broadcasting have recommended- that the C.B.C. shall have control over the operation of even its own network. I take it that this section takes away from the C.B.C. and gives to the new board the power to determine the amount of time affiliated stations should be required to use in broadcasting C.B.C. network programs.
The Fowler commission had something to say on this very important point on page 120

of its report, and I quote from this report because it has a very definite bearing on this clause. The report reads:
Once a network has been established and the affiliation of private stations with it has been approved, the operation of that network should be the exclusive responsibility of the C.B.C., subject only to the general supervision of the board of broadcast governors. The C.B.C. should have the power to prescribe the periods to be reserved by any private affiliated station for the broadcasting of programs produced or obtained by the C.B.C. The C.B.C. should have full authority to get programs forming part of the national broadcasting service out across Canada, over both C.B.C. and affiliated private stations.
And further:
We think that, as in the past, the C.B.C. should have the necessary authority to operate the national television and radio networks it has been authorized to establish.
As I read it, this clause takes away from the C.B.C. authority over its own network. The Fowler commission, also I think on page 120, recommended that the C.B.C. should have power-and someone has to have that power -to decide when a program is of such national importance that it should be carried by all the private stations, and I should like to ask the minister whether that has been changed also by clause 11.

Clause 11, the power to make regulations, includes, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, power to determine the minimum broadcasting time to be reserved for network programs by any broadcasting station operating as part of a network. The board of governors undoubtedly has power to make regulations in such a matter, and generally to prescribe the terms and conditions for the operation of broadcasting stations as part of a network, and all the rest of it.
We shall come to the network in a short time, I hope, and there the powers are specifically spelled out. No change can be made in any network in which the C.B.C. is interested, or to which it is affiliated, without a public hearing to which the C.B.C. is invited and at which the corporation is given an opportunity to be present. There are three powers with respect to networks: first, compelling a station to come into a network, making it a condition of getting a licence that it shall become part of a network; second, taking a station in operation and compelling it to become part of the network; and third, providing that the board may at any time upon the application of a licensee revoke or amend the condition after a hearing.

Subclause (d) of clause 11 provides that the board may make regulations:
-respecting the proportion of time that may be devoted to the broadcasting of programs, advertisements or announcements of a partisan political character.
I should like to say at once, in order that the question may be before the committee, that I wish to move an amendment to this clause which would read as follows:
That section 11 (d) be amended by deleting all the words after "progress" and adding: "of a partisan political character, the same regulations to apply to each individual station, whether privately or publicly owned."
I should like at this point to say a word or two about this proposed amendment, because I want hon. members to be well aware of what I intend the effect should be. It would mean that the same regulations with respect to compulsory broadcasting for political purposes would apply to private stations as apply to public stations.
It seems to me the justification for this is that the whole of the broadcast area is a public domain. The private stations have franchises but they do not have any absolute property, as the minister knows; and it does seem to me that it is in the public interest, particularly in the television field, in view of the fact that there are public stations only in five or six places in Canada and private stations elsewhere, that the same rules should apply in both.
That is not the case now. It has not been the case during the last two elections, and that situation has led to some very bizarre results. I am not going to waste the time of the committee by enumerating them. However, there is another and more serious problem in this field. I think every member of parliament of whatever party must be concerned about the growing cost of elections in this country, the growing sums that political parties and candidates have to raise by one means or another-and I am not going into that-in order to get themselves elected. And it does seem to me, further, that here we have a part of the public domain, something which belongs to the whole of the people of Canada, and one over which this parliament has jurisdiction.
While I have never been completely satisfied with the apportionment of the time allotted by broadcasting and television stations-I do not think any political party has been completely satisfied-I have never thought that it was grossly out of proportion. However, if we were to apply the same rules to both public and private stations that would eliminate the undesirable competition which now goes on during election periods to buy up great quantities of time, boring the
Broadcasting
listeners in many cases and increasing, to no one's real advantage, the already far too high cost of elections.
Don't you take well?

I am told there are people who are worse. I really do not fear this competition myself. All I am worried about are the bills that come in afterwards, and I think that is a common experience in this house. If we had one set of rules applying to both public and private stations there would be a great and immediate reduction in the cost of elections, a reduction which would be very much in the public interest and which would not be contrary to the interests of the stations, either, because my experience is that many of these radio stations do not like to have their normal programs disturbed to the extent they are disturbed during election campaigns by these competitive political programs.
I do not know too much about it, but I am told the stations charge much higher rates on that account than they charge to other clients, because it is temporary business; and I think we would all say "thank God for that". But here is something we could do in a completely non-partisan way which it seems to me would be good for parliament and good for the country.
I am putting this forward in as noncontentious a way as I can. It may be that the minister would prefer to have stand this amendment for a little while, and that in the meantime he would wish us to go on to consider other aspects of this bill, because I admit no advance notice of it has been given, and this is a very important subject. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that no one in any part of the committee would suffer any disability, that the broadcasting interests both public and private, would suffer no injury, and that it would conduce to a better atmosphere and a better standard of public life.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Chairman, perhaps in fairness to the hon. member I had better say something. This matter received a great deal of consideration by the various people who were working on this bill over a period of months. The hon. member knows pretty well who many of those were. Personally I think that it is unfortunate it is in here at all. I do not think the board of broadcast governors should be responsible for the allocation of political time. Consideration was given to various amendments.
I do not know how many hon. members know this, but under the C.B.C. regulations

Broadcasting
as they apply today if there happens to be a town council by-election in Wolfville or Port Alberni, then the C.B.C. is not supposed to broadcast political programs for three days prior to that by-election although there may be a provincial general election in Ontario. That is the existing regulation which has application to federal, provincial or municipal elections. The thing is just silly.
I do not believe the board of broadcast governors should be saddled with dividing or allocating this time any more than the C.B.C. should have been in the past. After a great deal of discussion we felt it might be allowed to stand this way; the elections committee of the House of Commons would be set up in the relatively near future, and that would be a much better forum in which to discuss this question and arrive at some solution with respect to political broadcasts and so on, rather than attempting to deal with it by way of amendments or by a board outside the control of parliament. That is why the regulation is as it is at the moment. I would suggest that the hon. member withdraw his amendment and allow the matter to stand over until next year, when something really has to be done about the whole problem.
Mr. Chairman, before I make any decision on that point I should like to ask the minister a question. As I read this, and it may be in the same language as the act-
It is; at least, I am told that it is.

Well, I have not checked it and I do not know either. Perhaps I should have checked it before I got up. As I read the clause it says nothing about allocation. I had the impression, which may be quite wrong, that under the Canadian Broadcasting Act the board was expressly charged with the responsibility of allocating time as well. It may be that was done simply by the extension of a phrase such as that contained in this clause; I do not know. It would hardly appear to me that this language by itself would give the board of broadcast governors power to allocate time as between parties, for example.
I am a little perturbed as to whether we are going to leave a gap in the law here in this statute, because we are repealing the Canadian Broadcasting Act which gives that body the power to allocate time, and in this bill we do not seem to make such a provision. I can find nothing in the bill to that effect, although the minister may point out that I am wrong. We are repealing that provision of the existing law and in this bill we have

put nothing in its place. That would be a very serious step for this parliament to take, because it would mean no one would have that power until there was further legislation. I do not think any of us anticipates a federal general election between now and the next session of parliament, and much as I would like to see a change of government I do not feel I would be in favour of a general election at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You might lose your seat.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
You might be
decimated.

However, it might very well be that before the next session of parliament a general election would take place in one of the provinces. I would think we would be acting in a rather irresponsible fashion in this chamber if we were to repeal the present law respecting the allocation of time and put nothing whatever in its place. I wonder if the minister would give some consideration to that point.
I should like to take a second look at that. We will let it stand for the moment.
I should like to have my amendment stand for the time being, until we see what is the situation.

Under the existing law the power concerning allocation of time is contained in section 21, subsection 1 (e) of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, which reads as follows:
The corporation may make regulations-
(e) to prescribe the proportion of time that may be devoted to political broadcasts by the stations of the corporation and by private stations, and to assign such time on an equitable basis to all parties and rival candidates.
I know there was a great deal of discussion while the drafting was going on about the unpleasant task of allocating time as among the parties. They wanted to avoid that, and that portion was struck out. I will check with the officials on that score.

It is an unpleasant task, Mr. Chairman, but someone has to do it; and until parliament prescribes some other method I feel we should put back the language that is in the Canadian Broadcasting Act. Perhaps the whole clause could stand for the moment.
Yes, it could stand until after one o'clock, and in the meantime I will speak to the officials.

If things are as the minister stated in regard to Port Alberni and Wolfville, why did he leave clause 17 (d) as

it stands? As to his suggestion that this be considered by the committee on elections, I believe that could be quite unfair from the point of view that we have C.B.C. provincial networks. As the minister may be aware, our committees represent the general proportion of the house so far as parties are concerned but there may be some places in Canada where the C.B.C. has provincial networks where this proportion would not exist at all, reflecting the provincial set-up. If the committee of this house has the power to do things of this sort, it would have the power to work against the political situation in a province that is not reflected in this house at all. I wonder how much the minister has thought about turning over to the committee on elections of this house the determination of both the character of political programs and the amount of time and the allocation of time?

The thinking was more negative than positive. The thought was that we did not want to start fundamentally changing the law with respect to political broadcasting in this bill because we might be tied up for a week on a discussion of all sorts of suspect motives which might be alleged. The thought came to us that probably referring it to the committee would provide a better medium, although frankly I never thought of the point the hon. member just raised, at least in so far as federal broadcasting is concerned. Referring it to the elections committee was a very good excuse for not trying to cope with those clauses at the moment but to bring forward the sections from the old act into the new bill for the time being.

I wonder if I could direct a question to the hon. member who moved the amendment. Is it his intention that the amendment should put the private stations in exactly the same sort of situation at election time as exists in the C.B.C.; that is, that there will be a division made by some central place of the amount of time the private stations shall allocate to the various candidates? If that is so, how does he propose to reconcile the fact that the C.B.C. divides the time roughly in proportion to the number of candidates, the number of votes and that sort of thing, whereas in a private station you get the amount of time for which you are able to pay? It seems to me you have two things in conflict there, and I am wondering about the intent of the amendment.

I do not know if this is a regular proceeding, Mr. Chairman, but since the question interests all of us I might reply in part. The hon. member put his finger on it at the very end of his statement; it is the amount which you pay. In moving this 57071-3-201
Broadcasting
amendment my thought was that there should be nothing more paid for time on private stations than could be paid for time on public stations, and that whatever regulations apply would apply uniformly to public and private stations. There are certain areas in this country where we have only public stations, and where local broadcasts are given during election time. There would obviously have to be different regulations for the broadcasts of the national political parties and of the individual candidates; that is quite obvious.
I have not worked out a scheme in any great detail, though I have given an enormous amount of consideration to the subject. I am not going to trespass on the time of the committee by giving my views on it at the present time. I feel that this is the public domain and that it should not be necessary for members of parliament or political parties to pay any more for time on private stations than on public stations.
I quite agree with the latter part of the hon. member's remarks, Mr. Chairman, but 1962 is an election year which this particular group is looking forward to with a great deal of anticipation.
Oh, oh.
We feel that for the first time in that election we shall have the money to play an equal part in buying time on private stations.
Where are you going to get it?
Is this what the hon. member means by his championship of small business?

Mr. Chairman, I understand that the proposed amendment has been allowed to stand. If that is so, I wonder whether the minister would care to comment on paragraph (b) of section 11, dealing with standards of programs. It is a serious matter and the hon. member for Port Arthur, for example, attempted to illustrate it. What yardstick will the board of governors use to establish those standards? Will there be a board of censors created; will there be a board on morals; will there be a board of artists and musicians? I would appreciate it if the minister will inform the committee what yardstick, what basis, will be used for establishing the standards of programs as envisaged in section 11, paragraph (b).

I cannot answer that question, Mr. Chairman, except to say, as has been said time and time again, that we propose and hope to choose Canadians, men and women across this country, representing the

Broadcasting
nation as a whole, and it will be left to their judgment as to what standards will be set. 1 certainly would not think we would ever reach the time when there would be censorship imposed except that which is imposed by the good taste and good judgment of relatively average Canadian citizens across this country, though it is always a threat, as I gathered an offer was made last night which was stopped because of the violation of the rules.
I thought it was rather a unique situation that the Leader of the Opposition and the others who were here were very ably contending that we may be threatening to interfere with the C.B.C. in some way, and another hon. member followed by attacking me because I had not imposed censorship on the C.B.C. This is a problem you always have when people who feel it is justified are looking for censorship. Perhaps it is justified. Once you accept that for one thing which you think is right, somebody else may come along and ask for something which you think is wrong, and freedom is gone completely.
I do not think censorship should ever be imposed, and I am quite certain that any board which this government chooses would not be one which would want to impose censorship in the language which the hon. member used.

I do not think anyone on this side last night or on any other occasion ever advocated censorship of the C.B.C. One member, the hon. member for Port Arthur, did advocate in very strong terms that the C.B.C. itself should use better judgment in the selection of a particular program in the interests of better relations between Canada and the United States.

If I followed him, he
criticized me.

He criticized the C.B.C. for a particular program. I want to make it quite clear that no one on this side would advocate any kind of censorship on the C.B.C., of the kind mentioned by my hon. friend. The point, however, is a very valid and very important one. What are the standards which are to apply? I know the difficulty the minister is in, and we too would be in were it our responsibility.
Before I sit down I wish to go back to the minister's reply to my earlier statement. I want to be quite certain in my own mind that I understand exactly what he said. Perhaps he will tell me whether I am right in my understanding of what he did say. My understanding is that the minister has now said that the exclusive responsibility

of the C.B.C. for its own networks, something which was recommended by the Fowler commission, has now been altered and it is now subject to the control of the board of broadcast governors. At least in some respects that exclusive responsibility of the C.B.C. for its own networks has been altered.
I also understood the minister to say-it did not deal with my questions specifically, but I think it was implied in what he said- that it will now be the board of broadcast governors and not the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation who will decide that a program is of such national importance as to be carried by any private station. I take it that is a correct understanding of what the minister said in reply to me some time ago.

Subject to the sections to which I referred, I think that is a correct statement, Mr. Chairman. The C.B.C. comes under the general powers as enumerated in part I of the bill; but it should also be pointed out to start with that the C.B.C. takes over the new corporation, call it the board of directors if you like. It takes over, shall we say, holus bolus all the regulations, all the networks, everything which was established by the C.B.C. prior to the proclamation of this legislation. That will be taken over by the C.B.C. in its entirety and then changes may be made afterwards, if at all. They start with everything I have promulgated and everything which is a part of their system.

I would like to ask the minister another question which I think is of considerable importance. It represents, as I understand it, an exact reversal of the situation we have been discussing and have been asking the minister about. I refer to a situation where the C.B.C. did have certain powers which the proposed board of governors does not have. I can find nothing in this section, or indeed in the bill, which would give the proposed board the power which I think the C.B.C. now has to prevent stations from becoming members of networks operated by persons or governments outside Canada. As I read this bill, it will be possible under it, and I do not think it is possible at present, for a private station or a group of private stations to associate itself or themselves with networks or stations in the United States and broadcast-if I may use the expression-on the cheap by the use of United States program material. If that is the situation under this bill, and if this bill does not provide in section 11 or in some other section adequate guarantees in that respect, then we propose to move an amendment; but before we do that I would like to

hear whether my understanding is right. Perhaps after 2.30 the minister might enlighten us on this point.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.
Has the minister given any further consideration, not so much to the amendment I moved to clause 11 (d) as to the gap in the legislation?

I discussed the so-called gap in the legislation with some of the C.B.C. officials during the lunch hour. The gap to which the hon. member refers is found in the words "and to assign such time on an equitable basis". I am told that as a matter of practice that has not been done for some years by the C.B.C., and that it has been impossible to enforce it. I am told that they have brought those concerned together and tried to work out some agreement, but there is the difficulty of political parties and the difficulty of political groups, some of which may be parties and some of which may have had substantial representation but have now lost it. Altogether it was felt that it would place an intolerable burden on these officials to attempt to assign the time. I have no objection at all to the amendment in principle, but I simply say that as a matter of practice it has not been done for some years and the officials frankly think that it cannot be done.

The minister is speaking from hearsay but I can speak from something more than that, because I took part in the negotiations respecting the 1957 election on behalf of the Liberal party. I can say not from hearsay but from my personal knowledge that it was not possible to reach complete agreement on that occasion, as it was not possible before the 1957 election, and in fact the C.B.C. did eventually assign the time. I do not say they would need to use the power, but it seems to me that the power should be there in case it should be necessary to use it. Therefore I think the minister should consider putting back in for the time being the words that were in the previous statute, until parliament can do something else about it.
I am prepared to accept that, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It has been moved by Mr. Pickersgill that section 11 (d) be amended by adding the following words: "the same regulations to apply to each individual station, whether privately or publicly owned." 57071-3-261|
Broadcasting

On this point, Mr. Chairman, in view of what the minister has just said and in view of the opportunity we have had to air the matter, if the minister were prepared to give the assurance that at the next session of parliament the whole question of political broadcasting would, on the initiative of a member of the government, be remitted to the committee on privileges and elections for study with a view to making recommendations as to suitable legislation, because this is not the kind of legislation the government should design-
I am perfectly prepared to do that. I felt that I could not accept the amendment in the words in which it was phrased.

I recognize that. I should like to finish what I was saying. As far as my personal convictions are concerned, I believe this is a sound amendment; but I do think I would be subjecting myself and any of my friends who voted for it to the same kind of criticism to which we are subjecting the government over this bill if I were to press it at this stage. It does seem to me that this is a very big and complicated subject which should be properly studied by a committee before the law is changed.
