Having accomplished the purpose I had in mind of having the subject aired, I would be quite prepared, if the committee is agreeable to my doing so, to withdraw my amendment on the understanding the minister has already given us, that he or some other member of the administration will take the initiative at the beginning of the next session of parliament, and not in its dying days, to bring the whole question of political broadcasting before the committee on privileges and elections for study and report, and on the further understanding that the minister will move an amendment to this clause to put back the provision for the assignment of time.
Yes. I will have one of my colleagues move that the words "and to assign such time on an equitable basis to all parties and rival candidates" be added to subsection (d).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
May we get rid of
the first amendment? Is it the pleasure of the committee that the hon. member be permitted to withdraw his amendment?

Agreed.
Amendment withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
May we have the minister's amendment in writing?

Broadcasting

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
move:
That the following words be added to clause 11, subsection (d): "and to assign such time on an equitable basis to all parties and rival candidates."
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 11 as amended carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I wonder whether the minister has had an opportunity to look into the matter I brought up just before lunch hour, when I tried to point out that the power which I understood the C.B.C. has to prevent private stations affiliating with United States networks or stations, except for a special program, has not been transferred to the board of broadcast governors. I understand that there were certain stations, before the C.B.C. came into existence, which did have such an association or affiliation, and that was not interfered with; but when the C.B.C. came into existence it did not permit that kind of association with United States networks, except for single programs of national interest. I certainly would hate to do anything that would prevent, for instance, broadcasts of the world series.
However, I do not find anything of that kind in this clause or any other clause of the bill, which transfers that particular authority of the C.B.C. to the proposed board of broadcast governors; therefore presumably that kind of association or affiliation could take place.

I have not found the particular clause to which the hon. member refers. I think it was done by regulation under the C.B.C. and those same powers of regulation are transferred to the board of broadcast governors today. When we go on through clauses 11, 12 and 13, particularly 13 dealing with network programs, you will find that no network, in any way, shape or form can be operated, and no station can join a network, without specific approval of the board of broadcast governors. Although the C.B.C. will not have that power in the future, it will be vested completely in the board and will be exercised by that board.
So that in a sense the new board will have exactly the same authority as the C.B.C., if not in law then at least in practice?
That is right.

Paragraph (f) gives the board the power to compel licensees to broadcast network programs of public interest or significance. Does that mean that the board can compel private stations to incur a loss in carrying these programs, or are they recompensed from public funds?
[The Deputy Chairman.]
The board will have the power to compel stations to carry programs of public interest.
Yes; but at a loss, or is the loss made up in some way?

That would depend upon the facts of each case. The board is given the power under this clause to do things on terms and conditions, so it would be possible for the board, if they thought the circumstances warranted it, to make such an order under certain terms or certain conditions. In other words, perhaps the station could be paid if the circumstances justified it.

Subclause 2 again refers to a licensee. Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked the minister whether or not the definition of licensee was complete. I wonder whether the minister could tell us if a licence will be required other than under the Radio Act, because this is the Broadcasting Act. If the word "licensee" is intended to cover both acts, it should be stated that a "licensee" means a person licensed under the Radio Act and the Broadcasting Act, that is unless no licences are required under the Broadcasting Act.

The licence procedure is set forth in clause 12, which says that "the Minister of Transport shall, before dealing with an application under the Radio Act", so it is under the Radio Act that the licence is granted and that is why that definition is used in the interpretation section. This clause means a person licensed under the Radio Act. There is no change whatever, in that procedure, I understand, except that under this clause the licence shall be authorized on the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors rather than the board of governors of the C.B.C. Of course the hon. gentleman will appreciate also that there are many other licences such as those to the police and those who operate short wave stations,-that is why we were very chary about dealing with this matter-and all those things are under the Radio Act. We have left the Radio Act intact so far as this bill is concerned.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 12-Applications for licences to be referred to the board.

Prior to the last election I was in communication with the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. regarding the television situation in Pembroke, where the reception is very poor. I would like to ask the Minister of National Revenue, because I noticed that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked a question about this matter yesterday, whether it would not be

possible for us to secure a satellite in the Pembroke area. Reception in the territory from Codben west is exceptionally poor. I saw the warning of the minister that he is not prepared to deal with many of these questions, but I would ask for his sympathetic consideration in respect to this matter.

In the past the decision has been made by the board of governors of the C.B.C., and it will be made by the board of broadcast governors in the future. I said I had the advantage of knowing something about the satellite expansion program, and so was able to answer the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. However, if the hon. member will defer his question until my estimates are before the committee I shall deal with it specifically then.

There is a point in connection with licensing in general, and I suppose it involves policy, which I should like to mention. I wonder if the minister could tell us anything about it. There has been a suggestion that a private television station at Port Arthur may establish its own satellite, somewhat in the same way the Timmins station has established its particular satellite. I believe the people of the area generally would be very pleased with this, but not if that particular satellite, by taking care of one part of the nodal population, will mean that the whole population will not get television service through the C.B.C.
This brings up the point as to who is to make the decision when the C.B.C. should move into a certain area. If this particular station in Port Arthur puts up a satellite down along the north shore it is quite possible, given the power that it could set up in that very good location, that it will take care of the nodal population to the extent of 5,000, which was the standard set by the Fowler commission as being the least number practical from the point of view of setting up a transmitter. However, if the fringe area of this new satellite were to be included in another nodal area to the north, it would give more than a population of 5,000. I just wondered if the minister had any ideas as to how this very difficult matter could be handled.

I cannot give the hon. member a solution, but I can tell him the mechanics of it. If he looks at subclauses 3 and 4 of the present clause, he will find that we start off with the fact that no recommendation shall be made by the board on any matter unless it has held a public hearing at which the applicant, the corporation and other interested licensees have been given an opportunity to be heard. The first thing is
Broadcasting
that you have to have a public hearing before you can come to a decision.
Then I draw attention particularly to subclause 4. I believe it was the Leader of the Opposition yesterday who asked me if there was a reference somewhere to the public interest. If you read subsection 4 of this section you find this provision:
(4) No recommendation to issue a licence shall be made unless, in the opinion of the board, it would be consistent with the purposes of this part and in the public interest to do so.
So in the particular case to which my hon. friend refers the board, after hearing all the parties, will have to decide on the merits wherein lay the obligation in the public interest, and the decision would have to be made accordingly.

In this particular case as to the announcement the minister made a few weeks ago on the C.B.C. plans, they will have to come before this board of broadcast governors before any action is taken. Is that right?

I would not want to say definitely on that matter. Those plans are in process of fruition now, as I told the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. It would depend to some extent when the personnel are appointed and when the board is ready to take over. It may be in October or in November. In the meantime the plans for the C.B.C. for this summer I hope will be fairly well advanced. The new board will, of course, have to take this matter into consideration.

We hope those plans will go ahead. We would hate to see Kenora-Rainy River without its television station, but even there a problem arises. How are communities around Kenora-Rainy River, such as Sioux Lookout or Dryden and places like that, going to be informed or understand the fact that they could make certain presentations which would suggest that the station might be located a little closer to them or have a little more power? Now all we can do in line with that situation is just accept the fact that the C.B.C. in its wisdom and with the advice of its engineers is going to do the best possible chore. It seems to me that the establishment of any of these stations needs to call upon a fairly informed, let us say, public reaction in the area. I am just wondering how that can be done under the present set-up without hearings.

I do not know how it can be done without hearings. There will be hearings in future under the bill. At the present time I think registered notices go out, and so on. You will see in section 11, which we

Broadcasting
just passed, provision that every meeting of the board shall be advertised in the Canada Gazette and giving the reason therefor. I certainly realize that the Canada Gazette is not the most widely published journal in Canada, but at least it is usually read by newspaper editors and people generally who are interested in public matters. Certainly if a notice appears in the Canada Gazette I would assume that all local and weekly papers in the area concerned will make very plain that this hearing is going to take place, and give notice of it.

The minister has called our attention to subsection 4, which provides as follows:
(4) No recommendation to issue a licence shall be made unless, in the opinion of the board, it would be consistent with the purposes of this part and in the public interest to do so.
I should like to ask who can appear at a hearing of the board in order to protect or advance the public interest in respect of this matter. Under section 3 only licensees, as I understand this section, can appear at a public hearing. Licensees are the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or private stations. Under that section there is no provision for anyone else appearing at a hearing of the board except licensees. Therefore if some association-the radio broadcasting league or some organization of that kind-wished to make sure that its concept of the public interest was voiced at a hearing of the board, how could it be sure under this section?

There is more than one licensee. You have applicants, whoever they may be, for licences. You have existing licensees. It is not limited to the corporation; it is all existing licensees across Canada and the corporation, which is the C.B.C. This is a public hearing. It will have to be advertised in the Canada Gazette.
Frankly I am not sure, but I think there is another section somewhere in which provision is made for the public to be present. Certainly if any decision has to be made in the light of the public interest I think it would follow automatically that a board of this nature conducting such an inquiry would give ample opportunity to be heard to the radio leagues, boards of trade, town councils and everything of that nature. That is why we inserted the clause "in the Canada Gazette". Naturally licensees and the C.B.C. could be notified by registered letter, but we wanted to have it on a broader basis than that in order to meet the very point raised by the Leader of the Opposition.

That is true; but under the old act while there was no provision, as I

remember it, made for the public to be represented at a hearing in the way you have suggested, there was also under the old act no limitation on those who could appear at public hearings. If I read this section aright, however, such a limitation has been definitely included, because under this section the hearing will be limited to the corporation and other interested licensees. But section 2 defines "licensee" as meaning only "a person licensed under the Radio Act to establish a broadcasting station". No matter how many licensees there are there is no provision for any others than licensees appearing; therefore there is a limitation on the right of the public interested to be represented before the board, a limitation which was not included in the old broadcasting act.

I have not before me the similar section in the old act, but I can find it. I think the answer to the thought expressed by the Leader of the Opposition is contained in the first clause:
(3) No recommendation shall be made by the board on any matter referred to it under subsection (1) unless it has held a public hearing-
I direct attention to the words "a public hearing". I think it would follow as a matter of law, and it certainly would follow as a matter of practice and common sense, that a public hearing would not be limited to just one, two, three or four parties. Certainly it is the intention, and I have no hesitation whatever in saying this, to include any interested party, and that is the whole basis of it. Perhaps if we had 500 crackpots or something like that, coming in to stall for a month of two, the board naturally would have to use a little reason, but any responsible organization or individuals will be given full opportunity to appear at a hearing of the board before any licence is granted.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This section is one which falls to the determination of the Minister of Transport. It authorizes the issue of licences under the conditions set out in the section. I am concerned at the moment about two matters. I wonder whether the minister would not give them consideration, or tell me whether they are covered by this section. The first is the assurance that in granting these licences, either for broadcasting or for television, there be a Canadian content in the program. I am sure that is a matter that will commend itself favourably to the minister, but in view of the discussions that took place during consideration of the resolution and prior thereto I think there should be no hesitation in giving the house the assurance that, in so far as licences are concerned, either those which will be granted or those

that have already been granted, the programs shall have a certain Canadian content.
The other point I want to bring to the attention of the minister is that which has to do with association by new stations with networks outside of Canada. The tendency might well be, as I have put it in the house on more than one occasion, for a station that is not operating profitably or for a station that wants to operate more profitably to enter into an agreement with a network outside of Canada whereby it can pipe into this country canned programs which would be deterimental to the culture of our country. I have in mind now particularly stations in the province of Quebec where, because of the particular culture of the people, it would be easy for a station that was not being operated profitably to bring in canned programs from the United States or elsewhere, for that matter, which would have a content which would be detrimental to the tradition and culture of that province.
I am sure the minister would be the last person who would want to see a condition such as that exist, so I summarize what I have to say with reference to these points by asking him if it would not be possible in the granting of licences to add a condition which would provide, first for the assurance of Canadian content in the program, and next for the assurance that no station or network other than the C.B.C. might associate itself with a station outside Canada except in certain circumstances, for instance where a single program is the national interest.

As far as Canadian content is concerned, the board is given power to deal with the Canadian content of any program, and in clause 10 it is also laid down that the whole object and purpose of the board is to establish a service of high quality which is basically Canadian in content and character. Under the provisions of clauses to which we shall come in a minute or two the board has such power to control the establishment of networks as might be necessary as far as the Canadian content of programs is concerned.
I am not quite sure what the hon. gentleman meant by "having programs piped in", but as he knows there are many stations, not only in Quebec, which carry, shall we say, canned programs of recordings having a minimum Canadian content. I hope this situation can be improved as time goes on. But whether they are recordings or whether they come in by wire, I am sure the hon. gentleman believes, as I do, that the Canadian content should be increased and that we should not allow such things as he has described to happen.
Broadcasting

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the situation now with reference to the Canadian content so far as the C.B.C. is concerned?

Perhaps the hon. gentleman could address that question to me when the officials are here, or when my estimates are before the committee. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is already familiar with this, but the study made by the Fowler commission a year ago shows that the amount of Canadian content is basically unsatisfactory in many situations where many dollars have been made. Sometimes it is in reverse proportion, the more dollars the less the Canadian program content.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Has the minister given any consideration to making either of these two matters which I have brought up a condition precedent to the granting of a licence?

No, I have not, except that the board has that power, of course, and I have no doubt that the board will exercise it. Again, this is a matter which I think we will have to leave for the board to decide in its judgment.

There is one thing I should like to add to the minister's answer with regard to the C.B.C. When applications for new licences are considered the board are quite firm about the content of the program; they examine programming very carefully, and they are very strict about the Canadian content.
It is difficult to police it.

They are very thorough, though, concerning new applications. I am not able to say what happens after the stations are in existence, with regard to the content of programs then, but the question is dealt with specifically and firmly when application is made.

The many provisions which have been included on the subject of licences might have indicated what the government thought about the problem which would be facing the board of governors in connection with the establishment of television stations in the richer markets. This will raise many difficulties. I wonder-and here I admit I am fishing for information-why it was not thought fit to put in something more definite as to who should get a licence for a station say in the Toronto area. It seems to me that without any clear instructions the board of broadcast governors is going to be in the devil's own position in determining who should get it. Maybe that is as it should be, and maybe the board is so constituted that it can handle

Broadcasting
this problem, but I should like the minister's views because this is one of the crucial questions dealt with by the bill.

The hon. member said he was on a fishing expedition, but I think the fishing season in Ontario has closed. The procedure is laid down here, but again I think the hon. member and I are at cross purposes to some extent, because he referred before to instructions to the board with respect to regulations and now he has mentioned instructions with respect to the granting of these licences. Certainly the last thing I should want to do would be to take any responsibility with respect to the granting of these licences in any circumstances. That is a matter which will be determined by the board in accordance with the machinery laid down here, and decisions will have to be made by the board in accordance with what they consider to be the public interest.
Here I hope the hon. member is not unwittingly confusing two things. Certain areas are restricted. That has nothing to do with the C.B.C. at all; that is a matter of policy which was decided by the previous government and which has been unchanged by this government. If any change should be made there will be an announcement to that effect.
That announcement would be made by the government?
Yes.

The minister said he would be the last person who would want to have anything to do with the granting of licences. Of course under this legislation he will not have as much to do with it as the Minister of Transport-
I will not have anything to do with it.

But if I read the subclause right, it leaves the final approval to the governor in council, of which the hon. gentleman is a distinguished member. In other words the final decision as to the granting of licences rests with the government. That is quite in accord with the recommendation of the Fowler commission, and I have no criticism to make of that.
However, my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo, who is detained elsewhere by a meeting I should like to say something about if the rules of the committee permitted it, did raise a question which I think is rather important. We all know that under the present law-and, I assume from my reading of clause 12, under this bill-it is competent for the governor in council to reject a recommendation of the board of broadcast governors. The question the hon. member for 
Burin-Burgeo asked me to raise is one which the minister may perhaps be inclined to dismiss as academic, but I am not sure that it is academic; I am not sure there is not a loophole here which should be filled in. Let us assume that a licence has been applied for and that the board has considered the application and recommended against it. Could the governor in council, under this legislation, grant that licence if it wished?

No. My understanding is that the governor in council could not grant a licence unless there was a recommendation by the board. I think that is the practice, and I think that is what was done under the previous board, with one exception of which the former minister is probably aware.
I wonder if the minister could remind me of the exception, because I confess I do not recall it.
Possibly the hon. gentleman was away in Newfoundland at that time. It was in connection with one licence which was granted, I understand, against the recommendation of the board.

But the minister is quite satisfied that this would not be legally possible? I am not saying that the governor in council would be likely to do it, and I did not know that such a thing had ever happened. But if it could happen we should surely guard against it.

I think the machinery is well established that the licence is granted on the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors. I do not think it necessarily follows that the governor in council is obliged to accept that recommendation. He might exercise a veto and say, "Go back and make another recommendation".

I am not questioning that at all. What the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo was concerned about was this. These licences are applied for through the Department of Transport. Presumably they go from there to the board of broadcast governors and back to the department. I imagine the Minister of Transport does not bring them to the governor in council at all if the board does not recommend them, but 1 am still not quite convinced from reading the clause that it would not be competent for the Minister of Transport to bring them to the governor in council and for the governor in councii to approve them if it saw fit to do so. I would think that would be an undesirable possibility to leave in the statute.

Clause agreed to.

On clause 13-Affiliation with C.B.C. network at time of issue of licence.

Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago the minister said in regard to the issue of a licence that he did not like the idea of laying down conditions precedent in a bill. I am not quarrelling with that, but I notice that in subclause 1 of clause 13 the board may recommend that a licence be issued subject to the condition that the licensee shall operate the broadcasting station to which the licence relates as part of a network operated by the corporation. I am not objecting to that condition, but somewhere in this bill I would like to see-and I have raised this question before, as have other hon. members on this side of the house -a condition of that kind in reverse; in other words, that there be a similar condition either in this paragraph or some other place in the bill which would be to the effect that the licensee shall not operate a broadcasting station to which the licence relates as part of a network operated outside Canada. If we can lay down a condition to the effect that it must operate as part of a network in Canada, surely as a means of protection we can lay down a similar condition that a licence shall not be granted except on condition that the broadcasting station will not be operated as part of a network owned outside Canada. Does the minister not agree that it would be desirable somewhere in this bill to state that it would include this condition precedent, just as we now have the one contained in this clause?

I think that is desirable, but I believe it is covered by the bill. I do not like to be leapfrogging ahead but clause 14, though it does not specifically say it must be in Canada, specifically spells out the fact that a licence can be granted for a network or a station only to a person who is a Canadian citizen.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 14-Applicant to be Canadian citizen, etc.
Mr. Chairman, when I first read paragraph (b) of this clause I thought there must have been a printer's error.
Yes, it looks that way at first glance.

It now reads:
(b) a person lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence who, since being so admitted, has been ordinarily resident in Canada for a period of not more than six years.
If that person, not a Canadian, resides in this country for five years, or even four, three, two years or one year, he qualifies
Broadcasting
for the issue of a licence; but if that foreigner in this country resides here for longer than six years he will not qualify. Is that not the situation?

No, Mr. Chairman. With respect, I believe the Leader of the Opposition has misconstrued it. The applicant has to be a Canadian citizen. I admit that when I first saw this clause I thought it was a typographical error, but this is an indirect approach without spelling something out. That is what it amounts to, to be perfectly frank. I believe the former minister of citizenship and immigration knows exactly what is involved in this. The paragraph reads:
(b) a person lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence who, since being so admitted, has been ordinarily resident in Canada for a period of not more than six years.
In other words he has to be here six years but not one, two or three years as the Leader of the Opposition suggested. The theory of that is this. Under the law a person lawfully admitted can become a Canadian citizen. He has to be a resident of Canada lawfully admitted for five years; the former minister of citizenship and immigration can correct me if I am wrong. Then he may become a Canadian citizen. We have added one more year and said, "If you are here six years and have not become a Canadian citizen, you do not deserve a licence. You should take out your citizenship." That is why the indirect language is used. It is to prevent people from getting licences who have been residing in Canada long enough to become naturalized Canadians, and we give them one year in addition.

I understand that now, Mr. Chairman, but surely it still means what I said it means, that an American here for one year can qualify for a licence, but if he has been here for six years and has not become a Canadian citizen he does not qualify. This means however, that a foreign licensee or corporation operating a station in Canada could continue the foreign operation of that station by changing its owner every five years.

I do not wish to argue about the legal interpretation. I am quite certain the Leader of the Opposition is wrong, and certainly if he is right the lawyers are not. From the language of the clause which I have already read into the record I think the intention is that they cannot grant a licence to someone who has been here for only a year.

It would appear to me that once a person is lawfully admitted for permanent residence-that is to say as an immigrant, not a visitor to this country-under

Broadcasting
this provision he could apply for a licence. The board could do what it pleased about his application, but it would be perfectly proper for the board to grant it up to the sixth anniversary of his landing or the sixth anniversary of the time he became ordinarily resident, which is not always quite the same thing. When I read this I wondered if it were directed specifically against Mr. Hal Banks, but I might be wrong about that.
I can see why it has been put in. I suppose it would be somewhat unreasonable to say that a British immigrant who had been here for four years could not get a licence because he had not been here for five years, or that a United States citizen who had been here four years and who had every intention of becoming a Canadian citizen as soon as our laws allowed him to do so could not go into the broadcasting business. I do not know that I would disagree with that.
I believe this is a new provision. I believe the Canadian broadcasting legislation provides that a licensee must be a British subject or a Canadian citizen. What troubles me about this is that once having got the licence, could you keep it if you went on after the six years without becoming a citizen. I mean, you may get the licence before you have been here six years, but if you do not take out your citizenship, can you keep it? It seems to me it is the keeping of the licence rather than the getting it that is the substantial thing and that would be more offensive to what the Leader of the Opposition was talking about. Under this bill you might have some way of getting a licence before you were here six years and of remaining a foreigner and continuing to hold the licence, because there is no specific provision for cancelling a licence.

There is no provision for automatic suspension or cancellation of a licence. Once a licence has been obtained proper steps would have to be taken to cancel it. It would have to go on if none were taken. It does not say it automatically lapses.

That is precisely the point, Mr. Chairman, and the minister is creating a discrimination here. If you get the licence just before the six years are up you can keep it indefinitely, whereas if you do not apply for it until after the six years you cannot get it. Perhaps the minister would allow me to give an illustration. Let us take two United States citizens who have both been in Canada for seven years. One applied for a licence just before he was here for six years, and he would go right on having it. The other, because he did not apply until he was here for seven years, could not get a licence at all. That does not seem to me to be fair and reasonable.

I am intrigued. I was in error in answering the Leader of the Opposition. It is, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, possible to get out a licence in that interregnum. You cannot get it after six years, whereas you could previously. I think perhaps some attention should be paid to that point so there will be some provision preventing someone carrying on indefinitely.
Would it not be better if we merely returned to the provision which restricts the application to Canadian citizens? I have not the text before me.
Have you the section there?
Perhaps we can let this stand, Mr. Chairman, because as the minister has pointed out it does seem to be anomalous.
I suggest that we let it stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 14 be allowed to stand?

I have one more question. I have difficulty in understanding this, perhaps because of my lack of legal training. Subparagraph Cii) of paragraph (c) reads:
A corporation other than a corporation controlled directly or indirectly by citizens or subjects of a country other than Canada.
I am thinking of a company such as Famous Players Canadian Corporation, which owns what amounts to a controlling interest in one of our television stations. Would it be affected, as a matter of fact, by this as being itself a subsidiary of an American organization?

The subparagraph says:
A corporation other than a corporation controlled directly or indirectly by citizens or subjects of a country other than Canada.
I would not want to make a specific decision on any named company, but that is the intention.
The Depuiy Chairman: Shall clause 14 be allowed to stand?

Agreed.
Clause stands.
On clause 15-Board may order suspension of licence.

Subclause 3 of clause 15 grants the right to appeal against an order of the board on a question of law; but if a licence has been taken away or has been refused on a question of fact instead of on a question of law there is no appeal.
That is so.

Oftentimes the reason for taking away a licence will not be on a question

of law but because the station has not been administered according to the rules laid down by the board. There is no appeal whatsoever in that case, even though the station owners may have spent $400,000 to $500,000 on the station. Everything would be lost, because the station owners will not have the right to appeal.

This does not cover cancellations; it covers suspensions, as the hon. member says. It would have to be a drastic violation, or a flagrant violation of the rules and regulations, and then it has to be referred to the Minister of Transport. They have to wait 10 days to give him time to enter an appeal. Of course, also, the board is given power, if it wants to, to do things on certain terms and conditions and it could, if it saw fit, order the suspension on certain terms and conditions; therefore I think the licencee is protected. I think this is taken from the other act almost verbatim. It is a subparagraph which I do not think was ever exercised. It is a good one to have in the act to assure some compliance with the regulations which will be laid down.
It is similar to the right of appeal given to the pipe-line companies.
Yes, it is comparable.

I agree that it is a very wise provision to give a party the right to appeal when the licence is cancelled. Is there also the right of appeal from a decision of the board when it refuses to grant a licence?
No.

I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that such right of appeal should exist. I do not think that right of appeal should be denied to anyone who has complied with all the regulations and formalities and requests the issuance of a licence. If the board refuses the licence the applicant should have the right that is given to everyone under normal circumstances and by the rule of law to seek redress from the courts, to have his day in court, because I do not think any board could possibly be considered as a board of final jurisdiction.

I cannot agree with the hon. member on that. There are scores of boards of this nature where appeals are not allowed, including the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The legislation has been in effect throughout the years. An applicant appeals to the board and the board exercises discretion, in its wisdom. It refuses the licence, and there has been no appeal to the courts from
Broadcasting
that decision. The hon. member would undermine the whole basis of the independence of the board if appeals to the courts were allowed in each case.

Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat at sea with respect to this section, because when I look at section 18 I find that it reads:
Every person who violates any of the provisions of this part or the regulations is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction as provided in the Criminal Code.
It seems to me that anyone who has his licence suspended must have violated the regulations. I just wonder how you equate the two things. It does seem to me that anyone who breaks the regulations is liable to have his licence suspended and also to conviction under the Criminal Code. I bring up this point because I notice that the Fowler commission in the draft act put these two items very close together in their suggested sections 27 and 28, and they specify the fine. Can the minister clear up my turmoil in this regard?

The Fowler commission also points out in the report that it would probably be impossible to get a conviction. I think that is true. Let us take, for instance, the standard of programs. How are you going to convict someone for failing to maintain a standard? I think any lawyer in the house would welcome the opportunity of defending rather than prosecuting, but there might be some violations which could be prosecuted in the courts. This is a relatively simple provision that is included in most acts. It is simply a summary conviction. In other words, you cannot prosecute by indictment.
These are the two regulatory or enforcing provisions in the whole of this bill. One deals with suspension. As I said, it would only be used in the most flagrant case. The second deals with the right to prosecute, under which the prosecuting counsel would have the court deal with the advertising content or what regulation it was. How are you going to measure it? It is a good thing to have in there. It has a salutary effect. Frankly, that is the purpose of it.

Subclause 3 of clause 15 brings a question to my mind. A while ago the minister said it would have to be a very serious infringement of the regulations that would bring about the suspension of a station's licence, but there is nothing in this section or in the legislation anywhere which states that. It is left to the board, and the board may, depending on how they look at it, be severe in some instances and less severe in others. Does the minister not think it would be a lot more democratic to permit an appeal on a question of fact so it could be proven

Broadcasting
in court whether the board was right in suspending the licence or whether it was wrong? The licensee would be satisfied if he had the right to appeal from the board to a court which could overrule the decision of the board.

I cannot accept that. I do not think this danger which the hon. member for Hull sees will arise. I go back to the fundamental statement I have made 50 times in this debate. If you have the right personnel you are not going to run into the difficulty which the hon. member envisages. If you have the wrong people the act fails anyway and there is nothing we can do.

The minister refers to having the right people or the wrong people and he may be right but these people may have different views on various matters. They might act severely against some people and less severely against others. There is no recourse whatsoever to protect the rights of these people.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 16-Operation of station as part of a network.

Clause 16, as I understand it, gives the government a very good opportunity if they desire to take advantage of it, and I think that they agree with this in principle, to provide for the contingency I have mentioned two or three times, that a Canadian station may affiliate itself with a foreign broadcasting network. I put this point to the minister because I should like to get an opinion on it from him before I decide whether to move a formal amendment. The clause now reads:
(1) A licensee shall not operate a broadcasting station as part of a network unless-
I suggest to the minister that there might be a new condition which would be first in order and would read as follows: "A licensee shall not operate a broadcasting station as part of a network unless (a) it is a Canadian network."

According to my understanding, under clause 14 there has got to be Canadian control in any event. I cannot see any objection to the suggestion made. On the other hand, I do not want to accept it at the moment because there may be peculiar circumstances. There may be times when Canadian stations are connected with foreign networks for the purpose of carrying service programs such as presidential addresses or election returns in Washington. There are scores of such programs where Canadian stations operate as part of such a network for a relatively short time, and an absolute

prohibition such as the Leader of the Opposition suggests might interfere with that. With the intention that the network should be Canadian, I would rather see the matter left to the judgment of the board for the moment and more consideration given to the technical problems which might arise if you had an absolute prohibition as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On that point, I do not wish to repeat what I said earlier but I think such an amendment would meet the two conditions to which I suggested the minister should give consideration, having to do with the granting of a licence for a broadcasting station or a television station. If this amendment were accepted by the minister it certainly would meet any difficulties I found myself in with respect to the point I raised earlier. Surely at first blush it would seem that there should be no objection to this condition because this is the clause under which a licensee shall not operate until and unless certain conditions obtain. Therefore I am going to press the minister respectfully to allow the clause to stand and give it consideration in the meantime.

I want to get through with the bill some time. As the hon. member points out, a licensee shall not operate a broadcasting station as part of a network unless (aj it is a condition to the licence issued in respect of the station that he do so. In other words, he has to apply to the board of broadcast governors for permission to operate, shall we say, as part of a United States network. That procedure has to be followed, everybody has to be notified and the machinery gone through to which I referred a few moments ago. I cannot believe that the board will be granting licences of that nature, certainly not in the immediate future. What conditions may be as to affiliations and networks in this rapidly changing industry I do not know. As I have said, we do have temporary networks. I think the clause should be allowed to stand as it is. It is pretty specific and certainly more definite than the old act. Undoubtedly it was covered to some extent in the old act but it was not spelled out as directly as it is here. You just cannot get permission at all to join such a network unless that condition is specifically endorsed on the licence that you have the right to do so and so. I should think it would be very difficult to obtain endorsement of such a condition.
As I have said, this is a technical field and I do not feel free to make commitments, although I agree entirely in principle and I feel sure that the principle will be maintained in the foreseeable future. Nevertheless I do not want to agree to something which in the end

might prove embarrassing and difficult to administer and perhaps might reflect on the conditions here.
I appreciate what the minister has said and I am not pressing him-
Bring it up in January before the committee.
-to amend the bill in a hasty way which might have results that we do not contemplate.
That is right.

I am also pleased to hear him say that this kind of condition would in fact be attached by the board to the issuing of a licence and that the board would have no intention of issuing licences to stations which would operate as part of a United States network, which is something different from being associated with such a network for a particular program.
In addition to ensuring that Canadian networks and stations remain Canadian, we also had in mind the protection of the board against the kind of pressure that might be exerted on it to sanction this kind of affiliation and if the words I have suggested were included in the bill they would be a protection for the board. However, I think the minister has stated the policy of the government very clearly in this regard. He has, I understand, said that this is a matter which should have consideration as one of primary importance by the committee when it is set up next session. In the light of this assurance by the minister, perhaps we can let the matter stand.
That is why I am anxious to see the committee set up at the next session, so that we can deal with some of these things having had a little more experience than we have had now.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 17-Political programs.
This, of course, is the famous Mr. Sage clause that some of the older members of the committee will recall.

I am not so old and I
remember it.

I presume it is in precisely the same form as it is in the present broadcasting act. I have not checked it word for word but I would not have thought that the minister would lay profane hands on it without telling us. It is, of course, a travesty in its present form. I am very familiar with the legal opinion that Mr. Dunton got from the Department of Justice about this matter. It did not satisfy me and
Broadcasting
I do not think it would satisfy anyone else who had any regard for the English language, but it was probably good law just the same. In its present form, apart altogether from the question in the minds of some of us whether or not "dramatized" is a verb at all, we do know that all kinds of practices go on at the present time that can only be described as dramatized performances.
One of my colleagues mentioned to me a moment ago that in one constituency in the last election a hockey game was paid for by a candidate not a member of this party and every so often the candidate appeared to put in a plug for himself. I do not know whether or not a hockey game is a dramatized performance but I would think it was certainly not the kind of political broadcasting contemplated when clause 17 was put into the present act. I am not going to suggest any amendment but I should like to have the assurance from the minister that clause 17 will be specifically remitted to the committee on privileges and elections for study during the next session.

It was the understanding when we inserted it here rather reluctantly that this was not the place to include it but as this certainly was not the time to engage, as I said before, in a prolonged political discussion about advertising and programs it was put here, shall we say, as a temporary resting place until the elections committee could meet.

The minister must have considered the fact that under the provisions of this clause he is putting the Prime Minister in danger of violating the law because the Prime Minister, on more than one occasion, has broadcast, in a highly dramatic form, programs, advertising and announcements of partisan political matter.
That type of program would not be banned.

Following the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with respect to clause 17 (1) (a) which does not permit a dramatized form of political program, I may say that I have not much criticism of that because in my constituency they have mostly been tragedies.
I do want to refer for a moment to this paragraph (b) which says:
No licensee shall
(b) broadcast a program, advertisement or announcement of a partisan political character on any day that an election is held for the election of a member of the House of Commons, the legislature of a province or the council of a municipal corporation, or on the two days immediately preceding any such day.

Broadcasting
I want to bring an incident to the attention of the minister and ask him if he does not think this clause requires amendment, and whether it might be one of the things to be studied by that committee which he suggested. In the last election political candidates would go across to the United States and give addresses over United States television stations which would be received in Canada and re-broadcast in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, by people who have licences to pipe in television or something of that sort. Would this clause not require amendment? The candidate or some person goes outside of Canada and uses United States television facilities, then that program is picked up in Canada by a Canadian who has made an arrangement with the corporation and has a licence from the board to broadcast piped-in television. How are we going to avoid that? It does not affect our party because I am told it costs about $100 a minute and about 15 minutes would exhaust our funds. Would the minister say whether or not he considers there should be some change?
Obviously that is a violation of this clause. Obviously the clause should be repealed and a new one substituted therefor, after discussion with this committee.

I do not quite understand the wording of paragraph (b) and the wording in subclause (2). Paragraph (b) says:
No licensee shall
(b) broadcast a program, advertisement or announcement of a partisan political character on any day that an election is held for the election of a member of the House of Commons, the legislature of a province or the council of a municipal corporation, or on the two days immediately preceding any such day.
Then, subclause (2) says:
A licensee shall immediately preceding and immediately after broadcasting a program, advertisement or announcement of a partisan political character, identify the sponsor and the political party, if any, upon whose behalf the program, advertisement or announcement was broadcast.
If a station has not the right to broadcast such a program, why should they identify the sponsor?

That means any program, whether it is one week or two weeks before election day. Then you have to say that this program is sponsored by such and such a party, and so forth. The clause is identical with the one that has been in the act for 15 years. However it works, it is there.
Even if it was there, it may be dangerous.
Does the minister know how most of the municipal candidates describe themselves partywise in carrying out this provision of the act?
In Quebec we have school boards and they have been forgotten.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 18 agreed to.
On clause 19-Report to parliament.

This clause requires the board of broadcast governors to report within three months after the termination of each fiscal year to the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated by the governor in council for the purpose. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reports to the Minister of National Revenue.
He happens to be the minister designated.

Yes. There is a further provision in part II that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will report to the minister. It is possible that the board of broadcast governors will report to one minister and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will report to another. As has been stated a number of times in this debate, there is a good deal of misgiving that this very thing might happen and might tend to divide the Canadian broadcasting system into two parts, and that this is opposed to the one system concept of the people who have the public interest at heart.
We should like to see this section amended so it would specifically provide that the report should be made to the Minister of National Revenue. We do that because that is the minister to whom the C.B.C. has been reporting. We also do it because of the occupant of the portfolio at this time. We say that the Canadian people generally, while they may in various degrees question the government's attitude towards the national broadcasting system in this country, do have a good deal of faith in the present Minister of National Revenue. It has been said, in any public speculation as to the differences that might have existed within the Conservative party at one time on this issue, that the Minister of National Revenue could usually be counted upon to champion the cause of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and a national broadcasting system. It could be argued, of course, that the present minister will not always occupy that portfolio. If there is a cabinet post in the government that is considered more important, more of a plum, we would wish him well as he goes up the ladder.

However, we are willing that the board of broadcast governors should report to him, and in view of the long history of the C.B.C. reporting to the Minister of National Revenue we feel that should be made an operating part of this measure. If these suggestions were adopted we would then endeavour to have part II designate that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation shall also report to the same minister. Our group believes that this clause should be amended in order that the report might be made to the Minister of National Revenue.

I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for As-siniboia. I have some hesitation in supporting an amendment which would change a bill because of, shall I say, personal considerations for the occupant of a particular post in the government. If we were to carry this too far we would perhaps cause the minister to lose his job. I do suggest it is a bad principle to change legislation for these considerations.
However, we have other objections to this clause, Mr. Chairman, which perhaps I should mention. This clause 19 fails to require the board to report on broadcasting in general and on the performance of the component parts of the broadcasting system in particular. It merely requires the board to report on its activities. If this particular clause remains as it is at present all that the board will be required to do under it is to make an arithmetical recital of its activities, the number of meetings, what was dealt with, and that kind of thing.
On the other hand, under section 36 of the bill the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is required to report on its operations. That introduces a distinction of the kind we are so worried about, namely a distinction between the privately owned and publicly owned parts of the system. Therefore, in order to avoid that distinction we think that this section should be amended. Earlier I had thought that perhaps this amendment could be introduced to section 11 having to do with regulations but perhaps this is the best place to do it, namely section 19 which deals with reports to parliament. I should therefore like to move:
That section 19 be amended as follow:
By deleting the words: "on the activities of the board under this part for that fiscal year", and substituting: "under this part for that fiscal year on the performance and financial affairs of privately and publicly owned stations and networks.
I think this amendment would improve the bill. It would ensure that parliament each year would get a report from this board, not merely on its activities but on the operations of broadcasting in Canada, both on the part of public and private stations. It would be a
Broadcasting
far better basis for consideration by any parliamentary committee than would the kind of report which seems to be visualized in section 19. I would commend this change at least to the sympathetic consideration of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I could not accept this amendment in the words in which it is moved. A report under this part for that fiscal year on the performance of privately and publicly owned stations and networks is something to which one might give very careful consideration. But the amendment also requires a report on the financial affairs of privately owned and publicly owned stations and networks. Of course the financial affairs of publicly owned stations and networks are public property anyway, I presume; that is the corporation and its affairs are controlled by this parliament. But I do not know how far you can spell out, to use a slang expression, the financial affairs of a privately owned station. You will recall that Mr. Fowler in his report said that there should be but very sketchy information given by the board on the financial affairs of privately owned stations; that they should collect it and perhaps use it for purposes of program evaluation and so on but that nothing more than a balance sheet, I think he suggested, should be published, if that, so that rival stations and competitors would not be given access to the private affairs of the private stations. Certainly I do not think the committee would want to accept this amendment in the way in which it is worded.
As to the word "activities", I suppose there will be a report at the end of this fiscal year for part of it; if the board gets operating this fall, it will have to submit a report next spring. If there is some objection to that word "activities" or if there is some significance to it or something else is thought better, I am prepared to consider it. But I cannot consider the wording of the amendment as it is before us.

Would it meet the minister's objection to the wording if I made this suggestion? I appreciated his objection. Suppose the word "operations" be substituted for "performance and financial affairs" so that the amendment would read "a report under this part for that fiscal year on the operations of privately and publicly owned stations and networks". I am sure the minister will appreciate that there is a report. The C.B.C. has to report on its operations under this bill. The board has only to report on its activities. The House of Commons, when it is considering broadcasting matters, whether in committee or in the house, will have before it as the basis for that consideration a report

Broadcasting
which will be required on the operations of the publicly owned system but no report on the operations of the private element of the broadcasting system. I appreciate what the minister has said about the inadvisability of those particular words. I am asking him whether this amendment would meet the situation:
A report under this part for that fiscal year on the operations of privately and publicly owned stations and networks.
Would that meet the point raised by the minister?

Before the minister replies, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I think the amendment that has been moved by the Leader of the Opposition is a very good one. I am talking about the general purport of the amendment. I think what has been said is completely true, namely that the board of broadcast governors should be asked to report on the whole broadcasting system of this government and all aspects of it and should not be confined to a report if its own activities. I have no quarrel at rll with the word "activities". However, I think the type of report which the board is to make should be clear. I think it would be a mistake to make it possible for the board to overlook completely, if it wished to do so, in reporting on its activities the question of the privately owned as well as the publicly owned stations and networks.
I might say to the Leader of the Opposition that before he suggested his own subamendment to the amendment I had already written into the copy that I have the same word "operations" but I had deleted a little bit less from his amendment than had the Leader of the Opposition. I had deleted only the words "financial affairs" so that it would read:
And substituting: "a report under this part for that fiscal year on the performance and operations of privately and publicly owned stations and networks.
I appreciate the very fair way in which the minister has considered this suggested amendment. With the further suggestion as to how the amendment that was moved might be further amended, the minister might consider the question whether he himself could amend this section or accept an amendment which would spell out the type of broad general report that parliament would like to see the board of governors make on an annual basis.
Question.

It seems to me that we probably are to get a report on the activities of the board which is very limited or very

narrow. But what we really want is something much larger. Do we not want a report on broadcasting in Canada? Is that not the thing we are seeking to get at? I wonder whether the minister would consider another suggestion, keeping in "the activities of the board" and inserting after that "and broadcasting in Canada" or some similar phraseology that would get us the fuller report on the whole subject of broadcasting which seems to be what everybody desires.

One other difficulty about this matter, in addition to the financial one, is the fact that by this amendment, if it were adopted, we are telling the board of broadcast governors just what it is to do. In other words, we are defining the regulations for them and saying "you must do so and so" under the regulations in order that you may report to parliament. Personally, I feel that the report of the board of governors should be along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa West, a report on its activities in such detail as parliament might require to make sure that it is performing its duties, spending its money wisely and so on and so forth. Certainly I think there should be included in it a general statement on broadcasting in Canada, on the stations and so on. I do not know what the machinery of this board is going to be, and I do not know how long it is going to take to set this board up. I do not want to insert into this an instruction that the board should report, say, on April 15 when, obviously, the board may not have had time to receive reports on the operations of radio and telecasting stations across Canada.
I suggest that this is a matter which is worthy of careful consideration, and I think it could be left to the committee on radio this winter, when we shall have the regulations before us, to consider whether these regulations are wide enough and to ensure that we do get an adequate report on broadcasting in Canada.

I just want to comment on what the minister has said. He said he had some difficulty in including in this bill a provision whereby the board would be required to report on its operations. What we are trying to insure in this and in other parts of the bill is that the corporation should not be placed at a disadvantage before this board. The minister has agreed it would be unfortunate if the corporation has to produce this kind of report to parliament while the private broadcasting stations have to make no such report to anybody.

Is that correct? After all, the corporation is a crown corporation. We have

to provide the money for it. Its whole financial affairs are, so to speak, naked before us. That is not true of the private stations.

I appreciate that, and the minister was quite right when a moment ago he took exception to the wording of this amendment because it might be interpreted as prying into the private affairs of private radio stations, which we have no right to do.
The minister has suggested once again that this is the kind of thing which could be considered in the committee on radio and perhaps, in the light of what he has said, we should be content with that. But I would point out this is the third or fourth time we have moved amendments and the minister has said: let us refer this to the committee. This confirms our feeling that had this bill been brought in a month ago all these things could have been discussed in committee and we should have had a much better bill in consequence.

Oh, let us not disturb this atmosphere of peace and kindliness. The Leader of the Opposition knows very well that that statement is incorrect. The reason I am asking that this be referred to the committee is, of course, because the board has not been appointed and the regulations have not yet been drawn. If this bill had appeared six weeks ago the regulations would still not have been drafted. In other words, there is nothing that the committee could have done in connection with this bill except, possibly, to ask the minister: who are you going to appoint? That is about all that could have been done. Do not let us be under any misapprehension that this is due to the bill coming in late. It is due to the fact that under the ordinary processes of government, whether this had come down in January or August, action would not have been taken until the government and the ministers had had time to draw a deep breath and give the matter more consideration than is possible during a hectic session. Thus there is no substance in the suggestion which has been made that this could have been dealt with in a committee.

To continue in an atmosphere of peace and kindliness, may I say that I still feel that if we had had this bill before us and considered it in a committee of this house it might have been returned as a much better bill than it is now. The minister has suggested that this can all be done next session. But by then we will have a new act before us, and the board of broadcast governors will just have been set up-there will not have been much time-and the committee will probably be confronted with just those difficulties which confront us at the present time.
Broadcasting
In so far as a comparison is concerned between the kind of consideration here in the house and consideration in a committee, the minister must realize that every time we now reach a clause here we are confronted with cries of "carried" as soon as we begin to discuss it. We are doing our best to point out what we consider to be weaknesses of the bill, as is our duty, even though we are not unduly pressing our viewpoint, because obviously that would not be desirable. However, in the spirit of peace and kindliness I am willing to withdraw my amendment, especially in view of the fact, that as the minister has pointed out the original wording was not very good.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman leave to withdraw his motion?
Agreed.

I appreciate the attitude of the minister that the substance of this amendment could be considered next session and that the amendment has a good deal of merit in it. However, at this time I wish to revert to the point I made when I first stood up to discuss clause 19. We do not like the possibility -indeed, I may say, the probability-that the board of broadcast governors and the C.B.C. will be reporting to separate ministers. We feel that this could lead to a great deal of conflict. We feel it could lead to a minimizing of the effectiveness of the operations of the C.B.C. We have confidence in the attitude of the Minister of National Revenue, and this group has confidence as far as the national system of broadcasting is concerned, but this confidence does not extend to certain other ministers of the government particularly in the light of their clear history in this house. For that reason, and also because although the minister was very generous in his attitude to other suggestions he did not seem to show the same leniency toward this amendment -perhaps he is just modest because he is named in it-I should like to move:
That clause 19 be amended by deleting the words "member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated by the Governor in Council for the purpose" and by substituting therefor the following words "The Minister of National Revenue".

We are not able to support this amendment for several reasons. Perhaps, having served in governments, we have not the same faith in political immortality as the hon. member for Assiniboia seems to have. That would be one reason. The second reason is that we do not think the purpose which the hon. member has in mind will be served by this amendment, although I have no doubt he is thinking of moving a similar amendment later on when he comes to the C.B.C.
The position we take is that there should be no minister to whom the C.B.C. reports;

Broadcasting
that the C.B.C. should, as the Fowler commission recommended, report to the board of broadcast governors and that the board of broadcast governors in turn should report to the government, analagously with the existing situation under the existing act. The principle in this legislation is wrong and we think it will be made even worse if the government is foolish enough to have two ministers. I do not think any more than the Leader of the Opposition does that it is wise. There is no connection between the duties of a minister of national revenue-not the minister but a minister of national revenue -and the particular responsibilities under this act. It is possible that the Prime Minister even before this act is proclaimed will recognize the undoubted merits of the present Minister of National Revenue and promote him to a more responsible sphere and if for example we were to find in his place the Minister of Finance, then where would the hon. member for Assiniboia have taken us?
I would rather leave this as it is and trust to the good sense and the good judgment and perhaps even a bit to the fear of ridicule of the Prime Minister in this matter. But as for the question of this resolving any conflict between the two ministers, we do not think it would have that effect. In the circumstances we do not believe it is a good amendment.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should say a word or two at this time so that if a vote is taken my colleagues will not feel they are hurting my feelings by voting against the amendment. I appreciate all the kindly things that have been said and I accept them. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out a few moments ago, there is no relationship between the C.B.C. as such or the board of broadcast governors and the Minister of National Revenue, and whatever the future of the present Minister of National Revenue may be-whether he attains a more exalted status or whatever may happen-the fact is that one should not definitely commit the administration of the C.B.C. to a specific minister.
Reference was made to continuity over a long period of time. Dr. McCann was the minister reporting for the Department of National Revenue-
Previously he was the minister of national war services.

Yes. I believe it is much better to permit the flexibility which is now provided for and enable the governor in council to nominate a minister to administer the board of broadcast governors. That minister may be the Minister of National

Revenue or he may be the Minister of Finance. Of course, it may even be the Minister of Public Works; who knows?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate spoke about our perhaps feeling that there may be political immortality when we are asking that a particular minister be named. Then he went on to say that if we named the Minister of National Revenue, we might be horrified at a later date to find that the Prime Minister had switched ministers and the new Minister of National Revenue could be the present Minister of Finance. That would be a development that would give us great cause for reconsidering the moving of this amendment. But our fear is that without it being stated in this clause it just might be the Minister of Finance and that fear has been bolstered by the words of the Minister of National Revenue who said there is one of three possibilities-
One of two; I was just giving an illustration.

Now it is getting worse. We want to see the clause amended so that possibility would not exist. I believe it is not a wise thing to have this board reporting to an unnamed minister of the crown, a minister who can be changed from time to time. I believe it is far more in keeping with having a board of governors doing an effective job to have stated in the legislation the minister to whom the board will report. The looseness and ambiguity of this bill of which the official opposition has made so much for so long a period is going to be supported by them in voting against this amendment because they will in effect be asking that this free wheeling rein be given to the government.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate also took it upon himself to put words in my mouth by saying that no doubt we had in mind a certain amendment to part II. The hon. member is a very congenial fellow. He is a very good and valuable member of the House of Commons and, if I may say so, I believe he is improving. However, by engaging in the type of forecasting that has preoccupied him this afternoon his conduct leads one to wonder whether he may not be reverting to the status he enjoyed some time before he began to show the improvement to which I referred. Even if the hon. member is a lawyer I could prove to him, as I could prove to any one who is a lawyer, from the evidence I have on my desk that it is not the intention of this group to move the amendment he suggested.

We believe it is in keeping with the building of a national system of broadcasting to have a specific minister named in this clause, to move an appropriate amendment to a further clause in the bill and to make it abundantly clear if these amendments are carried that parliament wants a single national system with certain components rather than a dual system such as could flow from this bill providing as it now does for these two bodies to report to separate ministers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Question.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 5; nays, 131.

Mr. Chairman, there is another point about which I wish to ask the minister. He will observe that in part II of the bill the word "minister" is defined in clause 21, paragraph (d) as follows:
(d) "minister" means the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada who is designated by the governor in council as the minister through whom the corporation is to be accountable to parliament for the conduct of its affairs.
There is no definition of the word "minister" in the definition clause in part I of the bill but there is a limited or partial definition of the word in clause 19 in part I which says:
19. The board shall, within three months after the termination of each fiscal year, submit to the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated by the governor in council for the purpose a report on the activities of the board under this part for that fiscal year.
That is the operative part of the clause.
The reference to a minister is found in the words:
-submit to the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated by the governor in council for the purpose-
Presumably, the purpose is receiving the report on its activities. The significance of that, as I read it, and the way in which it is drafted, is that the minister can only be designated under the act for the purpose of receiving the report. He cannot be designated for any other purposes and if I am right in that it leads us to the position that there is no minister answerable in the house for the activities of the board, and no minister to whom we can direct questions, and who will otherwise be responsible in the house for the activities of the board. I am sure that was not intended. Perhaps there is an answer to it, and I would like the minister to give me the answer if he can.

I am not sure but what that is not virtually the answer to it, Mr. Chairman. It is roughly or approximately the
Broadcasting
same situation as applies now to the minister for the C.B.C. I am the minister designated under the act for the purpose of the C.B.C. and I have two functions at the moment: one, to recommend payments over $25,000; and, two, to report to parliament for the C.B.C. I have forgotten all the detailed discussion that went into the drafting of this, as my hon. friend will appreciate. Perhaps I should have used it yesterday in reply to the Leader of the Opposition. This goes a long way to meet the charge that the board of broadcast governors is under the control of the government, or something of that kind. This section was phrased very carefully to avoid such a suggestion. They report to the minister but the board is pretty well- in fact, I would say I hope entirely-divorced and removed from control. It has to report to parliament and parliament, I suppose, can exercise control, I do not know; parliament can take such action as it sees fit. That is the way the thing is defined in the act.

My point is this. Under the C.B.C. part of the bill the minister is the minister through whom the corporation is accountable to parliament. In the first part of the bill the minister is not defined at all other than as contained in section 19. He may merely be designated for the day to receive the report and turn it over to parliament. There is no minister accountable to parliament so far as I know. Under all other legislation, through one method or another, there is a minister accountable to parliament and to whom parliament may look for information and the like from day to day. It is this point which concerns me. It seems to me there is an omission there. The minister should be accountable to parliament and he is not accountable.
