There must be someone to whom parliament can direct inquiries. There must be someone, for instance, who will present the estimates to obtain the money to sustain the board of broadcast governors.

That follows automatically in section 20 which says:
All expenditures for the purposes of this part shall be paid out of money appropriated by parliament therefor.
There has to be someone-

That is just my point; someone has to do it, but there is no minister responsible. Therefore, when we have supplementary estimates pertaining to this board of broadcast governors we have no minister to whom we may direct questions. There is no minister answerable to parliament. That is the point. I wonder whether the minister would give some attention to that point. I appreciate his remarks about the other aspect

Broadcasting
of it, namely independence from direction by a minister, but that does not answer the part as to the responsibility to parliament.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 20 agreed to.
On clause 21-Definitions. "Broadcasting".

Mr. Chairman, there is a feeling among some of us that there would be advantages to having the C.B.C. report to the board of broadcast governors. So that there will be no question at all about the control that the board of broadcast governors should have over broadcasting and to clear up certain divisiveness in the way in which it is set up, I should like to move:
That clause 21 be amended by deleting the present subparagraph (d) thereof and by substituting therefor a new subparagraph (d) to read as follows: "Board of broadcast governors means the board of broadcast governors as set forth in part I of this act and is the board to which the C.B.C. shall report."

Mr. Chairman, I have no
objection to this amendment; in fact, I approve of it. But would it not be desirable to let any change in the definitions part of this bill be held until we see what is going to happen to clause 22, because the definitions will surely depend on whether any amendment is to be made to the substantive clauses. While we may propose amendments to clause 22, surely it would be unwise to change the definitions until we see whether there are amendments to the bill. I suggest the definition amendments be held over until we see what happens to clause 22.

Will the minister agree to the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition that we let clause 21, the interpretation clause, stand and go on with the other clauses because some of us have some suggestions to make on the other clauses, and while they probably will not be acceptable to the minister, they might be. If he is agreeable and if the hon. member for Port Arthur will be agreeable to allowing his amendment to stand until we dispose of the substantive clauses we could come back to the interpretation clause.
Will we get through by five o'clock?
It might help in getting it through more quickly.
That is perfectly satisfactory.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreeable to let the amendment stand?

My colleague has no objection to this clause standing, apart from the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition. He

may have a point. The only thing we had in mind was that clause 21 comes before clause 22, and if you let clause 21 go by, which is the definition clause you will really get into a flap in the committee when you wish to look at it afterwards. I think this is probably the best way to proceed, namely let this clause stand and deal with the other one. After we have been successful with clause 22 we can come back to the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the committee to let clause 21 stand?
Clause 21 stands.
On clause 22-Corporation established.

Mr. Chairman, this is the clause of the bill to which we are most definitely opposed and which gives us the greatest anxiety. It establishes, or re-establishes, perhaps, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in a form which we consider unwise. We have some objection to take to the details of the various subclauses, but our main objection- and the minister will not be surprised to hear this

is that the corporation should be set up in this way with a board of directors comparable in nature and composition to the board of broadcast governors. We also object-and this objection has been voiced before-to the corporation reporting separately to the minister and through the minister to parliament rather than through the board of broadcast governors.
The first amendment we would move to this clause would be to subclause 1 which now reads:
There shall be a corporation to be known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation consisting of a president, a vice-president and nine other directors to be appointed by the governor in council.
Incidentally, the president and vice-president are appointed in a different way and for a different period of time than the other directors. We are opposing this kind of board of directors for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We do not think there should be this kind of board along with the board of broadcast governors. That is our basic objection. If it is not accepted as embodied in the amendment which we will move, we will have other objections to raise and perhaps other amendments to move to other subsections of this clause. But in connection with this basic objection, I am going to ask my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to move an amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I move:
That section 22, subsection 1, be amended to strike out all the words after the word "vicepresident" and substitute therefor the words "and

a secretary to be appointed by the governor in council on the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors."
Subsection 1 would then read:
There shall be a corporation to be known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation consisting of a president, a vice-president and a secretary to be appointed by the governor in council on the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors.
I might say in support of this amendment that it will bring the whole structure of the bill into conformity with the recommendations of the Fowler commission. The corporation will not be a corporation sole; the corporation will consist of three persons. I think it is desirable that it should consist of three persons. There seems to be no useful purpose in having these nine directors whose functions will be entirely redundant if the board of broadcast governors does the things that the Fowler commission recommended that it should do. If it does not do those things, we do not think there is any place for the board of broadcast governors, but the position we took on second reading, the position we took before the bill was ever introduced and the position we are still taking is that the structure recommended by the Fowler commission is not a sound structure for broadcasting in Canada and by this amendment we would be going a long way toward putting the bill back on the rails.

I just want to say that the government cannot accept this amendment. It makes a fundamental change in the whole concept of the bill to which a great deal of time and consideration have been given. I know the arguments pro and con and I could repeat them ad infinitum. I have weighed them in my own mind for a good many weeks and in the end the government decided that this approach was the better approach in setting up the organization. You can say that it is redundant, you can say a lot of things, but it appealed to the government as the best way in which we could inaugurate this system, by only making a change in name and instead of the board of governors the C.B.C. has had given it a board of directors corresponding in other ways.
As to the argument that the directors should be removed and that the corporation should be reduced to a corporation sole or corporation three, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has just mentioned, I was thinking yesterday, as all these arguments were being used about political pressure and all the rest of it, how much greater the pressure would be if there were no board of directors and if it was simply a corporation consisting of three executive officers. As the bill stands,
Broadcasting
the president and the vice-president are members of the board of directors. They have their associates there and, to use an expression used yesterday, they are insulated as far as it is humanly possible to do so. At least it is a much better approach than if there were no insulation at all. That is why I wanted to see a board of directors set up, and I think it will work. I know the experience in Australia and I realize the difficulty expressed in the old cliches about one being stronger than the other, getting in each other's hair and so on. But after all this is Canada. We have solved our problems in the past. We have adopted unique approaches time and time again, very often involving compromises with those followed somewhere else. We have made them work and we will make this work. I at least want the committee to give us an opportunity to try it and see how it works. We can then change it if it should be necessary.

Before the vote is taken I should like to point out to the minister that so far as his preoccupation with protecting the officers of the corporation from political pressure is concerned, a preoccupation which we share, surely the insulation he talks about and which he suggests would be removed if the nine other directors were abolished, would be supplied, and I would hope very effectively supplied, by the board of broadcast governors. I am not suggesting that the directors be removed and that the executive officers of the corporation be left defenceless in the face of political pressure. We would substitute the more effective insulation provided by the new board of broadcast governors for the kind of insulation they would get from this board.
Amendment (Mr. Pickersgill) negatived: Yeas, 20; nays, 72.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 22 carry?

Mr. Chairman, now that we have failed to secure a fundamental change in this section we are going to try to improve it in its present form. For that purpose I should like to call the attention of the committee to the fact that while the president and vice-president of the corporation are appointed for seven years the other directors are appointed for three years.
These other directors are appointed, as the minister knows, during good behaviour and that gives them some security against pressure. The president and vice-president, contrary to the position of the chairman of the board of the present corporation, are appointed to hold office during pleasure, whereas the directors are appointed to hold office during good behaviour. Under subclause 4 a director may be removed at any time by the

Broadcasting
governor general on address of the Senate and the House of Commons, and only in that way. The president and vice-president, holding office during pleasure, can be removed without that procedure being followed. We believe that this is a fundamental weakness of this particular clause and a danger to the corporation.
Without saying any more, because the minister knows our position on this, I should like to move:
That section 22, subsection (2) be amended by deletion of the words "during pleasure" and by substitution of the following, "during good behaviour".

I do not want to take up much time, Mr. Chairman. I simply say again today what I said yesterday on second reading, that the government cannot accept that amendment. I recognize the arguments that have been made, but this procedure appears in other government corporations as well. It is done because these particular officers, as I said yesterday, are executive officers charged with the responsibility of doing executive work. I think it is only reasonable that if they should happen to fail in doing that executive work, if they should be inefficient or anything of that kind, then the president and vice-president could be removed. It is a contingency against which one should guard.

I think the minister has made the thing even worse than it appeared from the simple language of the clause. As I understand it, and I would be glad to be corrected if I am wrong because I have not looked at the statute on this particular point, the general manager and assistant general manager of the corporation are appointed by the governor in council on the recommendation of the board of governors of the C.B.C. and not by the governor in council direct. They have a certain security of tenure which protects them from the government. Now we are going to make a radical departure by having direct appointments by the governor in council without the intervention of any other body. If I read the bill correctly, the governor in council can remove these people, as the minister says, if they become inefficient.
It is not the board of the C.B.C. that is going to determine whether they are inefficient; it is not the board of governors, it is the governor in council.
I did not say that.
It is quite clear that the power to remove is inherent only in the governor in council. It is the pleasure of the governor in council.
It certainly is not on the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors, but of the directors of the C.B.C.

It certainly is not, and wherever they may pick up the gossip about inefficiency, it is only the governor in council who can exercise that power because it is his pleasure about which we are talking. The government is doing exactly what the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, and is putting a couple of its creatures in the two principal offices and saying that the moment they displease the governor in council they may be removed. Otherwise, what does this language mean?
I must say I challenged the minister yesterday and he has had 24 hours to produce any other statutes in which this incredible language occurs. I say "incredible" because it does seem to me it is a contradiction in terms when you say you are appointed for seven years and that you are appointed during pleasure. I can quite understand a person being appointed for seven years during good behaviour, but what does the seven years mean if it is during pleasure? It means nothing. It is just nonsense. It may be that there is some poorly drafted statute somewhere else that got through parliament, as this one has not yet, without anyone noticing this fact, but this one has been noticed. It does seem to me that, since it has been noticed, and after all the professions we have heard from the government of their desire to keep broadcasting independent of the government, here they are insisting on putting two of their creatures in office and saying that they can be removed any time that they decide, in their own way, in the closet, that these people are inefficient. Perhaps they just do not like them. They have to give no reasons to anybody. It does seem to me that this is the very negation of independence. It is impossible to imagine that even the purest government in the world would not, sometime or other, do that. Of course, this government may not always be here. It may be that some day some other hon. gentleman or some other hon. lady may be occupying their position.
It is just conceivable that there may be some minister who would not like the looks of the president or the vice-president. It does seem to me the minister ought to give some further consideration before he advocates this step which really legally destroys the slightest independence of this corporation.

Of course, that is nonsense, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member talks about a closet, but there is no area of the government service upon which the spotlight of

publicity will beat down with a greater intensity than on this matter of the C.B.C. When someone stretches his imagination to the point where he starts talking about dealings in a closet, and so on, he is stretching it pretty far. I can say that I can see some merit in this argument, that the appointment itself made by the governor in council could be one thing in which there could be political influence or almost anything, subject to whatever the judgment of the governor in council happened to be at that time. But once you make the appointment, believe you me any government that would change this appointment, particularly in the light of the qualification of seven years in there, and in addition to pleasure, would be going a long way. I cannot conceive of circumstances in which it would not be done on the recommendation of the board of directors.
My hon. friends have made a very strong and telling case on the use of the words, but I think they are very far removed from the practical aspects. I do not want to spend more time on it.

Can the minister give us any case where this device has been used in legislation before, the appointment during pleasure for a fixed period, of officials who are, in the first instance, appointed by the governor in council on the recommendation of nobody else? He said there were other cases and I wonder if he can give the committee the benefit of his knowledge?
I was told that, but I have not the other cases here.

I do not suggest for a minute that the minister has any intention of doing anything of this sort; I never suggested that. However, we are not making laws for this minister, we are making laws for sometime in the future. The minister spoke about the letter of the law. My understanding is that the law is all letters and that when you go into the courts, the courts do not construe the mind of the governor in council, they construe the words in the statute. Now, the terms "good behaviour" and "pleasure" are very ancient terms in the law and they are very well known to the constitution. They have been used throughout this statute, except in this one place. It does seem to me if there is ever one place they should be used it is here. I would have had much less quarrel with this bill if "pleasure" had been used in connection with most of the other appointments and "good behaviour" in connection with this one. Here are the two operating executives, the very two people that we depend upon the most to keep this
Broadcasting
organization independent, and they are going to be discriminated against by having this stain put against them.
All the Leader of the Opposition is saying is that the words "during good behaviour" should be put in here. He is not saying that there should have to be an address of both houses. All he is saying is that the governor in council should appoint them "during good behaviour" for a period of seven years; and if the governor in council has any cause such as that which the minister suggested-I am sure inefficiency is not good behaviour- or if the government finds any cause for their removal which is inconsistent with good behaviour, there would be no bar to that removal in the amendment moved by my friend the Leader of the Opposition. But it seems to me that we should not easily allow the government to put this kind of legislation on the statute books.

May I ask, Mr. Chairman, whether it is the intention-I have not been able to find it in the provisions of this bill although it may be there-to provide that the president of the corporation should be the chairman of the board and preside over the meetings of the board? The minister has referred to him merely as the executive officer. But is he not also the chairman of the board and the one who presides over the board of directors?

I do not think there is a section spelling that matter out in detail in the bill. But I think it was taken for granted that where someone was not named chairman or if there was not a definite designation, the chairman would be the president.
That is true with regard to the board of governors; he is designated.
Yes.
There is nothing in this bill to designate any member of the board of the corporation as chairman of the board?
That is right.

The minister may be noble in his intention as to whether or not the president or vice-president will be dismissed during the tenure of office of seven years. The question is this. Can they be dismissed if they incur the displeasure of the government? That is really the test. If that is the test and if they can be dismissed if they incur the displeasure of the government, then I think we are defeating our objective for this reason. We are not insulating them and giving the corporation the independence that we intend to give it. There is that difference. The president and the vice-president can hold office during pleasure and the others can do

Private Bills-Divorce so during good behaviour. Why is there that difference? I wonder whether the minister can explain to the house why the two principal officers can hold office at pleasure and the others can do so only during good behaviour? There must be a reason for that difference. I should like to hear from the minister an explanation for that difference.

I gave it previously.

The house in committee on Bill No. SD-304, for the relief of Freda Levine Schubert-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, while 1 will say right at the outset that I will not oppose this particular bill, I should like to draw the attention of members of this committee to

certain facts in connection with it. This is a contested divorce and I feel that on that basis closer attention must be paid to the evidence which was before the Senate subcommittees, and that we should give it as close a look as possible.
First of all may I comment that this case appeared before the Senate subcommittees on two occasions and that finally the matter was referred to the full committee. On the first sitting the subcommittee consisted of five members of the Senate, and on the second sitting, of four. Those four had been members of the original committee. However, at the sitting of the second subcommittee, the hearing was adjourned sine die, and there was a final meeting of the subcommittee composed of six members, two only of whom were in attendance and heard evidence at the prior meetings. I would submit-
Would the hon. member give me the page reference for his last reference about six, please?

Page 11 of the report. In
those circumstances I feel the members of this committee are quite entitled to review the evidence, being in the same position as the final meeting of the subcommittee which made the recommendation to the committee of the whole on divorce.
I must admit, and draw to the attention of the committee, that the subcommittees which heard the evidence in the original instance had the benefit of observing the demeanour of witnesses and that, in a matter of this kind, is of considerable importance. However, I should like to go into the evidence a little bit to indicate that while, possibly, the conclusion of the Senate committee in this instance might have been correct, I have some very grave reservations as to the full weight of the evidence.
First of all, we are concerned with an incident in a small restaurant in Montreal on September 11, 1955, which is approximately three years ago. I had some difficulty in assessing the precise accuracy of the evidence of the numerous witnesses concerning what happened on that particular morning. For instance, three witnesses were called who do not profess to know French and they commented on a so-called admission of misconduct by an alleged co-respondent, the admission and conversation leading up to it having been spoken in French. There was one witness who understood French and there was some suggestion that he translated as the conversation transpired.
If we look at the evidence of the witness Strober which appears at page 31 of the committee report we find the man admits he does not know French. He testified that the 57071-3-262
Private Bills-Divorce co-respondent who was a waitress in his employ was an hour late. She gave as her reason that she had been in a car with the respondent. She apparently used the word "coucher" which the witness said he understood to mean "sleep in a bed". It was in this language she described her relationship on that occasion with the respondent. However, the witness also said she had been away in a car. There is some doubt as to precisely what was said and what happened.
I might point out that a great deal of the evidence of all the witnesses was as to what happened prior to the respondent being present. That is why I have considerable reservations concerning just how much validity should be attached to the evidence of these witnesses. It is difficult to know how much of the evidence was based on fact and how much of it was hearsay evidence. A considerable amount of hearsay evidence appeared to enter the case. I should like to draw the attention of this committee to these considerations.
The evidence of the witness Morin appears at page 35. At no time did he identify the date on which the adultery is alleged. He was extremely vague as to when he had heard the conversation referred to and there was no corroboration that he had acted as translator. He appeared to draw conclusions from words that were alleged to have been said in that he states, in effect, "it must have meant this" or "it must have meant that". He prefaced many of his statements with comments of that kind and there is little evidence of direct statements.
The evidence given by the witness Rittmer which appears on page 37, I would submit, contains a great deal of hearsay. This man clearly admits he does not know French. As a matter of fact, there is some suggestion that he is not too familiar with the English language either and so it is rather difficult to know precisely what he might have stated if he had fully understood either or both languages.
I wish also to make reference to an unhappy event that occurred. The plaintiff closed her case. The respondent who was under escort since he was serving a sentence in a Quebec prison met the case against him under advice of counsel by denying the allegations made. He denied his presence at the restaurant where these statements were alleged to have been made and he denied knowing the corespondent. Following the close of the case the committee adjourned its hearings and subsequently the plaintiff presented another witness, Marafino apparently in rebuttal to the evidence given by the respondent to the effect that he was not present or did not know
4142	HOUSE OF
Private Bills-Divorce the named participant. The committee had reservations about hearing this evidence. However, it was heard and subsequently there appears in the record of the proceedings a statement to the effect that the committee decided to disregard the evidence of that witness. I would remind hon. gentlemen that we are all human beings. Regardless of whether the committee felt it should disregard the evidence of the last witness called, the members of that committee heard the evidence and their minds may have been conditioned or influenced by that testimony. They should not have heard the evidence of the witness Marafino.
These are the reservations I have about the evidence in this case notwithstanding the fact that many witnesses appeared before the committee. On the basis of their demeanour the committee may have preferred to give weight to the witnesses appearing on behalf of the petitioner and to have disregarded the evidence given by the respondent. I feel, as an hon. member of this committee who is asked to pass on a bill of this kind and as a practising lawyer, that I must indicate my reservations as to the type of evidence which was allowed to be presented in this case and as to the manner in which it was presented. I believe great care should be exercised in these matters. As I said, I will not oppose this motion but I wish to draw these salient facts to the attention of this committee.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Edmonton West has brought out in a striking manner a point which should be of interest to all hon. members when we deal with these divorce cases. This is not an easy case; indeed, it is an extremely difficult one. Those hon. members who have read the evidence will recall the circumstances under which the husband and wife lived together. They will recall her constant difficulty in obtaining any support whatever from her husband and also the fact that a large part of his life has been spent in certain institutions in the province of Quebec. There was also the circumstance that when he appeared before the subcommittee on July 8 he did not have a lawyer. Statements were made by the witnesses concerning the restaurant incident and he did not cross-examine the people who made those statements. Subsequently when the case was closed it was decided to reopen it and the moneys paid by the wife to have the case brought before the other place were used to help counsel, who had been appointed by the subcommittee, in an effort to find the key witness in the case, the co-respondent, the waitress with whom he is alleged to have committed adultery. It was a difficult case from start to finish and I suppose any lawyer would have his reservations about it.


I know that in my own particular case, for instance, I have read it some four or five times. Perhaps they had little precedent to guide them but what did guide that committee of the Senate, I am convinced, was their desire to be fair to the respondent, a man who does not enjoy the normal freedom of other members of society.
The hon. member for Edmonton West brought forth facts which-after the house heard his eloquent speech setting forth the matters-may cause some doubts as to whether we should consider it. I would point out that this matter has received the most careful scrutiny over a period of days. As a matter of fact, the first hearing started on July 8, and it went on until August 6 before the Senate heard the final witness. As the hon. member has pointed out, the Senate decided to disregard the evidence of that witness because, I presume, he could properly have been before the subcommittee on a previous occasion.
The committees of the other house of parliament are charged with this onerous duty of listening to the witnesses in the first instance, assessing their evidence and determining the reliability and the credibility of witnesses. If ever there was a case in which everything turned on the credibility and reliability of witnesses and perhaps very little on the printed record that is available, I would think it would be this case.
Unfortunately, the practice of asking leading questions of the witness was used, such as, "What were you doing on September 11, 1955?" the date of the offence. This, of course, was direct prompting which would not ordinarily happen in a court of law. Apart from circumstances such as that I think the respondent was given every opportunity and the fairest of treatment over there. I think that the subcommittee of the other place, acting on its impressions of the witnesses they had before them and the witnesses they saw there, came to a conclusion. My hon. friend did point out that the case was contested there. It was contested there, but it was not contested before us.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the sponsor of the bill can inform the committee whether the minutes and proceedings of the standing committee dealing with this pipe line are available to members of the committee of the whole. Mr. Chairman, I cannot tell the hon. member. Perhaps the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Peterborough, could tell whether the minutes are available. At that time they raise their objections and they have the right to examine and cross-examine the various members of the firm who are there for that purpose. If I recall correctly, there was not a member from the group led by the hon. member for Assiniboia at the meeting. However, I will ask the chairman of the committee whether the minutes are available.

We did not have a reporter in the committee at that time to take evidence. It is very seldom that there is a reporter present to report evidence on bills of this kind, because the committee counts on the members being present to get the information.

Excuse me, the evidence was not reported so that it could be placed in the hands of members of parliament. Evidence was heard but was not recorded.
We are opposed to this bill. I am not going to try to block the house in dealing with it today; I merely wish to register a continued opposition to the passage of this bill.
As has already been said on a previous occasion, the Stanmount Pipe Line Company is wholly owned by the Imperial Oil Limited. Imperial Oil Limited is part of an international cartel. Imperial Oil Limited itself is a subsidiary of Standard Oil of New Jersey, and I do not think it is wise for parliament to increase the power of this international cartel as represented by the Imperial Oil Limited. I think the stand of the Imperial Oil Limited has been in complete opposition to the building of a trans-Canada oil pipe line to supply to the Montreal area oil from Saskatchewan and Alberta. I suggest the stand taken by the Imperial Oil Limited has been a narrow one and has been governed solely by the financial interests of the Imperial Oil, and it is an endeavour by this international oil cartel to maintain the Montreal market for oil from Imperial Oil and its associates.
The independent companies in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are most concerned that a pipe line be provided to the Montreal area. If passage of this bill might result in such a line being built that would be a strong reason why members should support it, but I think the very fact that Imperial Oil wants this kind of authority when it is. opposed to the building of such a line shows that the passage of the bill will not mean that the result I have suggested will be achieved.
Another reason we are opposed to the passage of the bill at this time is the pending report of the Borden energy commission. We are hopeful that the report will deal, in fact we are certain it will, in a comprehensive manner with the oil and gas problems of the nation. We think that in the light of whatever report is made members would be in a much better position to judge whether or not the passage of this bill is in the public interest. On the basis of the evidence I have now I suggest its passage is not in the public interest.
According to an Ottawa Journal report of last Saturday, which report was subsequently picked up by the Canadian Press, the interim report of the Borden royal commission on energy is likely to favour a pipe line to the Montreal area estimated to cost $375 million. This is a proposition which will receive the full support of the people of western Canada who are looking for markets at this time for their very important oil production. As a

Private Bills
result of a reduction in the United States market for Canadian oil there has been a substantial cut in the production of oil on the prairies and this has had adverse economic results on the revenues of two provincial governments and the welfare of the people of those provinces.
I notice that the hon. member for Calgary South is in his seat. He is an authority on this whole question. He has taken a great deal of interest in the problem and I am certain that he supports the opening up of the Montreal market for Canadian oil. If passage of the bill would bring that day closer I would certainly give it my support but I do not think its passage would in any way solve the pressing problems of the oil industry at this time.
There is another reason why I am opposed to the course being followed by Imperial Oil in seeking to obtain the power through the passage of this bill to build a trans-Canada pipe line to Montreal. I have in mind the report that the United States government, instead of moving in the direction of easing the restrictions against importation of Canadian oil, may in fact increase those restrictions and lower the quotas for Canadian oil entering that market. It has been reported in the press that secretary of commerce Weeks of the United States government has asked for a further survey of the oil situation in the United States and that new quotas are likely to be posted within the next 30 days. According to press reports in all probability this will mean a reduction of import quotas on oil allowed into that country. I express the hope that these reports are not well founded, that the United States will not take this action and that in a short time restrictions on Canadian oil entering that market will be removed.
But with this present and perhaps growing danger I feel that parliament should be directing its attention to solving the oil problems facing the nation and not giving further strength and powers to Imperial Oil Limited, part of an international cartel which in my judgment, so far as Canadian markets are concerned, is operating and acting in a manner detrimental to the welfare of the nation. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, we in the C.C.F. are still opposed to the passage of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say only a word or two because I recognize any lengthy observations on my part would only tend to satisfy the purpose of our good friends in the C.C.F. in that we would talk out the bill.

On a point of order, I think I made it quite clear that while we were opposing the bill we had no intention of blocking it at this or any other stage in the debate.

I hope that the hon. member will understand that if he and other members should continue to debate the bill until six o'clock it will not indicate, as far as we are concerned, a deliberate effort to block the bill. We are opposed to it but we are prepared to accept the decision of the house.

I was honestly mistaken and I make the necessary apology.
I should like to make two comments on the remarks made not only in this but in the previous discussion by the hon. member for Assiniboia. First, I think some reference should be made to the status of Imperial Oil Limited who, through the bill before us, are requesting the authority at some point to construct a pipe line. While Imperial Oil has on a number of occasions registered its protest against the eventual imposition of any controls which might effect a restriction of foreign crudes coming into Canada, I think most members of the industry and most members of the house, I hope, will agree that Imperial Oil is itself concerned with the marketing problems of Canadian oil.
The second point I should like to make is that while it is quite true that I disagree in some respects with their arguments that have been presented to the Borden commission and while I certainly continue to support moving more oil out of western Canada to Eastern Canada because of the absolutely essential necessity of providing assistance to the independent operators, until the Borden commission has reported I do not here challenge the evidence submitted to it. That is the responsibility of the commission.
To deal specifically with the bill, I feel that all the protection necessary is vested in the board of transport commissioners to give consideration to the economic merits of such a project, and there is no doubt in my mind that when the Borden commission makes its findings and gives consideration to the future establishment of an energy commission it will make some reference to the over-all programming of the development of oil and natural gas. This is their purpose under their terms of reference.
However, all this bill provides is the right of this company to appear before the board of transport commissioners. If we found that we were, today, becoming involved in the economics of this problem, then I would agree with the member for Assiniboia that the facts are not all before us. Certainly by the time the company concerned with this particular bill is in a position to move ahead with it, assuming they do, then it would become the responsibility of the proper officials, whether it be an energy commission or the present facilities of the transport

board, and they would have to make a decision. I am quite certain that the rights of both the oil producers and the people of Canada will be taken into consideration at that time.
Before I sit down I should like to close with the comment that I think the hon. member for Assiniboia is perhaps being a little unkind to the sponsors of the bill. I have not any particular reason to have sympathy for them, but he referred to the fact that parliament should not give Imperial Oil this further control over the oil resources of Canada. He says that the powers of this company would not be used really to develop the resources of this company but to further impede the development. Then, he said, too, that Imperial Oil is a cartel and that Imperial Oil had been blocking resource developments for years. I would remind him, as I am certain he knows, that it was this same company that drilled 107 dry wells, and some at a cost of $1 million, before the Leduc No. 1 was discovered and brought a good gravity crude into this country. I think it should be kept in mind that this is a company which employs Canadians almost throughout; it has developed many secondary industries from its refinery centres, and it has produced substantial prosperity throughout very large sections of Canada. They together with independent companies have brought Canada's petroleum industry to the peak at which it is today. I feel that this should be said in their defence. This is not a private cartel and the passage of this bill will not impede future development of oil or gas in Canada. The purpose of this measure is merely to give the company the right to appear before a properly appointed board to give consideration, at the appropriate time, to whether or not it is economically advisable to build a pipe line.
For these reasons, I think the people of western Canada and in particular the independent operators would have no objection to proceeding with this bill.
I am sure the hon. member for Calgary South did not mean to say that I had said anything unkind about the sponsor of the bill because the hon. member for Davenport is a good friend of mine.
Does he admit it?

He can amend that statement if he cares to, but from my point of view he is a good friend. I do not think the hon. member would suggest 1 have said anything unkind about him. I may have said some rather unkind things about Imperial Oil, but being a very large company with world-wide interests and being part of a well-known international cartel, I do not suppose my
Private Bills
small voice raised in the House of Commons will affect Imperial Oil to any real extent.
It has been argued that we do not need to be concerned unduly in passing this bill because before any pipe line is proceeded with there must be approval by the board of transport commissioners and that board will take care of the public interest. Even if that were the case, and the board could be relied upon to take care of the public interest, I do not feel that removes from parliament the overriding responsibility to see to it that charters which are given to companies are, in themselves, in the public interest. One of the reasons I have opposed the passage of this legislation at this time is not only the pending report of the Borden energy commission, but the weight of evidence which suggests that there is anything but a certainty that this company will need the powers in this bill before the next session of parliament. In other words, this is not emergency legislation required by this company in order that it may continue its development. speechtext: Some question arises as to residence qualifications in connection with this bill. Would the sponsor of the bill care to comment on that?

Yes, certainly. The reason this bill comes to us out of order in so far as the other bills are concerned is precisely the point raised by the hon. member. It was a point upon which the committee experienced some difficulty, and upon which

Private Bills
we had to consult with the law officer of parliament, Dr. Maurice Ollivier.
The circumstances are, Mr. Chairman, that the respondent is a native of Ontario. He did move for a brief period to the province of Quebec. The couple, when married, lived for a while in the province of Quebec. About 11 months ago, the wife was deserted and apparently the respondent returned to the province of Ontario, living in the city of Ottawa. The evidence on that point is not conclusive. Certainly his parents live in the city of Ottawa and certainly the petition and other papers in the case were served upon him there.
Those members who looked into this matter pointed out that in Beauchesne's volume the matter of petitions received a great deal of consideration. Dr. Beauchesne clearly states that petitions should not be presented to parliament here or at Westminster unless the petitioner has exhausted all other remedies and has no other place to go. Obviously that is the old practice. In this case it appears, at least on the face of it, that the petitioner -and it is the domicile of the husband which governs; the domicile of the husband is the domicile of the wife-should not have brought her case before parliament but rather should have taken it first to the supreme court of Ontario.
As the committee can readily appreciate, this was a matter of extremely important principle. For that reason we spent some time the other day discussing it with Dr. Ollivier. It is competent for parliament to act in divorce petitions from any province of Canada. But in recent years it has been the practice, since provincial divorce courts were established, to consider only the cases irom Newfoundland and Quebec. When this matter came up for consideration, since it was uncontested, nobody had raised the point except a few hon. members. I wrote to the solicitor for the petitioner in the city of Montreal and asked him if he would submit a brief on this point. We also had the benefit of a brief from Dr. Ollivier and his assistant Mr. Batt. In the brief of the petitioner's solicitor there was some argument to the effect that there was evidence from which you could gather that the domicile of the husband had shifted to the city of Montreal. Personally as I know the evidence, I may say that the wife said that they had established a home in Montreal; but the home turned out to be an apartment and the purchase of a building as such was not involved.
As can be seen, the committee was obliged to labour under a goodly number of difficulties in connection with this matter. We finally resolved it by deciding to report the bill back without amendment. I think perhaps

I can fairly state that the members of the committee, on looking at this evidence, felt that the Senate committee might have been justified in drawing the inference that there was domicile in the province of Quebec, or again that this was one of those borderline cases of a man shuttling back and forth over the boundaries; and that the wife might have gone to the supreme court of Ontario only to find that the supreme court might have told her to go to parliament. Whichever course she took might have been the wrong one, as you can appreciate. Hence, Mr. Chairman, that is the position in which we found ourselves. But the recommendation of the committee was unanimous that the bill go back before the house. I think the hon. members raised a very useful question and I hope that this report will go down to the bar of the city of Montreal so that the lawyers there will know that we are looking into this matter and were concerned about it in this case. I hope they will govern themselves accordingly in the future and at least present much stronger evidence than was presented in this case if they are going to rely on domicile in the province of Quebec.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there are a number of questions that come to my mind on this clause. Is it a new clause? What schedule under the Financial Administration Act does the C.B.C. follow? As the hon. minister knows, there are a number of schedules in the Financial Administration Act which make a distinction between various crown companies. For instance, the Canadian National Railways have powers, in so far as administration and the expenditure of money are concerned, which the national harbours board has not. While the Canadian National Railways must come to parliament each year for an appropriation of funds, the position concerning the national harbours board is somewhat different. It also is another agency of the crown. It approves of certain expenditures and they go to the treasury board and receive concurrence there. Will the minister tell us in what schedule of the Financial Administration Act this falls and, for instance, what are the differences rinancially between the new crown corporation and the one which existed heretofore?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
I did not have the category in mind, but I did have the classification. I am advised by the officials that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation falls in schedule D and, as the hon. member will recall, that is the one under which the greatest freedom is exercised in any of the crown corporations. I have that particularly in mind because a question arose with respect to insurance, whether it came under the insurance act under which crown property is insured or whether it did not. It was suggested that we should move into another category in order to get the benefit of that act, and I registered objection to the C.B.C. moving to another one because I wanted to

maintain it in the highest classification of all and that, I am told, is schedule D. That is where it has been throughout the years when the hon. gentleman was responsible for administration as one of those on the treasury benches.
The other question he asked was as to the moneys. As he knows, the financial situation is this. Under the present act, under which we are operating, the minister must recommend all expenditures to treasury board and thereafter to cabinet, if it should go to cabinet, involving more than $25,000. Under this bill, if adopted, that ceiling is raised from $25,000 to $100,000, so that in the future the minister responsible for reporting for the C.B.C. will have to recommend expenditures only over $100,000. From that has been excluded any moneys to be paid for programming or program material, so that there will not be any suggestion of any influence by the government or the minister on funds for programming on program material although, of course, the C.B.C. will have to operate within the over-all budget which is provided for it by parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: The first question I asked was, is it a new section?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: No, this actually is not a new section. There may be a slight redrafting. The hon. member understands there are some implications, perhaps, in this section on various problems which could arise, which we are anticipating in this, but essentially it is exactly the same section as heretofore. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I see some danger in clause 28 where it speaks of the delegation to an executive committee of all or any of its powers. If the corporation can appoint an executive committee from amongst the directors, it can appoint a committee of part-time directors. It can take three or five part-time directors and even exclude the president, the vice-president and the third permanent director, and those part-time directors can be constituted as an executive committee and as such can be given all the powers of the corporation, if they so desire. I can understand that it is necessary at times to delegate powers to an executive or to some officers to do certain things, but I should like to caution the minister that this clause as it reads now makes it possible for five of the part-time directors to receive the delegation of all the powers of the corporation, which is somewhat dangerous. If such a thing theoretically were

to take place, then five part-time directors would be serving continuously at the rate of $100 a day, as provided by the act. I therefore point out this possible danger to the minister and ask him whether that is really the intention. I cannot read the clause in any other way except that it is possible to take five of the part-time directors and delegate powers to them and they could sit continuously at the rate of $100 per day, which is certainly far beyond what I am sure the minister anticipates. Therefore, 1 suggest to him that he re-read this clause and study it once more very carefully in the light of the observations which I have made.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I would refer the hon. member to section 31 which gives the corporation power to make bylaws respecting the calling of meetings of the corporation, the conduct of business thereat, the duties and conduct of the directors, officers and employees of the corporation, and generally for the management of the affairs of the corporation. In other words, the executive committee will, if appointed-and I presume one would be appointed-be subject to the bylaws which will be passed not by two or three directors but by the directors as a whole. I can assure the hon. member that there is going to be no danger that three or four part-time members on this executive committee will be sitting here in Ottawa drawing $100 a day or anything of that kind. The whole matter will be controlled by the bylaws of the corporation which actually is what has happened in the past. They will be bylaws under which the board of governors can set up committees and delegate authority, and we have taken the provision of the existing act almost word for word.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Does the minister not think he could avoid it if he simply said that the executive committee should consist of at least a certain number of permanent directors and, say, only two of the part-time directors, if necessary? If it is left wide open as the clause now reads, the minister can easily see that five part-time directors could be appointed as an executive committee, which I know the minister does not intend to happen.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Section 9 of part I of the bill has to do with the executive committee of the board of broadcast governors consisting of three full-time members and four part-time members appointed by the board. This is not followed with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which has a board of directors of which two are 57071-3-263J
Broadcasting
full-time personnel and the rest are parttime personnel. There does seem to be some real difficulty with the clause as it now stands.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
There is a difference there. In the section dealing with the C.B.C. we are following pretty well the existing C.B.C. legislation. Bear in mind, these are directors who are going to be responsible for the business administration. Primarily the thinking of the government in appointing this board of directors is that they will be responsible for the business administration and the details, and so on, of the financial operations primarily of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Now, my hon. friend refers to the board of broadcast governors. There you are dealing with a national body engaged in great questions of policy, shall we say, and the government wanted to make it abundantly plain that there would be a majority of non-permanent members there so as to avoid any suggestion that this was going to become a narrow, small group controlled, shall we say, by the permanent officials in Ottawa. Really, it is because of that, because of the difference in the function, that I think the board of directors who will be businessmen primarily appointed to look after the affairs of the C.B.C. can be trusted to lay down regulations and bylaws which will cover meetings of directors. The government had it spelled out in the legislation that with respect to the board of broadcast governors there ought to be a quorum consisting of non-permanent members, and so on.

I should like, not that I think it will do very much good, but in order to bring the bill a little more in line with what was recommended by the Fowler commission, to move:
That section 35, subsection 2, be amended by inserting the words "and current" after the word "capital" in line 15.
The clause would then read:
Within one year after the coming into force of this act and every fifth year thereafter the corporation shall submit to the minister and the Minister of Finance for submission to the governor in council a five-year capital and current program proposed by the corporation together with a forecast of the effect of the program on the corporation's operating requirements.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
This was a matter of policy which was decided upon by the government. It was decided that with the expenditures for the C.B.C. running to $60 million and $70 million, according to the Fowler commission, within a year or two that these moneys should be reported and passed upon by parliament. This does not mean there will be any different procedure than there has been heretofore. There will be a vote towards the operating deficit of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that has been done for some years. The treasury board has had to approve of all these matters.
We propose to carry on the same policy with respect to the current expenditures as was carried on by our predecessors throughout the years, except a year or two when the excise tax provided sufficient moneys with which to carry on all of the operating expenses of the corporation. I believe that this is an improvement, at least it is a step in the right direction over that practice which prevailed heretofore because you get this capita] budget approved by the governor in council and a forecast of the effects of that program on the corporation's operating requirements. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would, therefore, have in front of them an estimate, approved by the government of its capital program and a forecast of the effects of that on its current program, and with these two safeguards it should be relatively easy, subject to the vicissitudes of economic conditions or wars and other developments which one cannot foresee in the immediate future, for the C.B.C. to plan its program better in the future than it has been able to do in the past.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
The minister would not expect that travesty on the history of the corporation to go unnoticed. The minister knows quite well that every royal commission and every parliamentary committee that has considered broadcasting, and has considered this question, has taken the view that it would be undesirable to have the C.B.C. financed by annual appropriations. He knows that this was emphatically stated by the Massey commission and a scheme of financing was laid down by the Massey commission, which was implemented by the previous government over the opposition of hon. gentlemen then sitting over here, to give the C.B.C. an assured budget for a period of five years.
The question also arose of whether there should be a television licence or whether some other method of financing should be found for television, and the government had sought to find some means of financing which would be automatic and which would not be under the day to day control of the treasury. It was decided, as I indicated last night on second reading, to earmark the excise tax. Mr. Abbott introduced a bill which was opposed by hon. gentlemen opposite but which was passed by this house and which gave, until about two years ago, to the C.B.C. sufficient revenue of an assured character which was not under the control of the government.
Regrettably over the last year or two, because of the relative decline in revenues from the excise tax and because of the growing cost of adequate television coverage for the country, it became necessary for the government of the day, a government of which I was a member, to make annual appropriations. But we did that as a pis aller, realizing that it was a bad way to do things but that an emergency had to be met. As I said before that was the principal reason that the Fowler commission was appointed, and the Fowler commission, in the most emphatic of all its recommendations, recommended that the C.B.C. should be independent financially of annual appropriations, and that it should have an assured income with a maximum and a minimum so that it could plan ahead and so that it would not be subject to the day to day control of the government.
I realize that it is not competent to anyone on this side of the house to make the kind of amendment that is embodied in any of the financial schemes outlined in the Fowler report. However, it seems to me that the amendment which I have suggested and which does not involve any expenditure but merely involves the preparation of a five-year current budget as well as a five-year capital budget, would at least give to parliament and to the public the C.B.C.'s idea of what its
Broadcasting
needs were for the five-year period; and to that limited extent, at any rate, it would be a slight amelioration of what is a thoroughly bad scheme. It is for that reason that I put forward the amendment, not because I think this amendment will make this a good provision but rather because I think it will make this provision slightly less objectionable.

The league is disappointed that the bill makes the C.B.C. dependent on annual grants from parliament. The provision for a five-year capital draft program is an improvement. But it is not enough. Broadcasting
program for the next four years so that those responsible for dealing with financial aspects of policy will have that in mind and possibly see the benefits, I should say, in the future, as a result of this projected program of having the financial arrangements for a longer period of years.

As I have said, the general principle which the hon. gentleman has in mind in his amendment is something with which we can all sympathize and I trust that some day we will get a levelling off so that we can project expenditure. However, I should like to call the attention of hon. members to these figures which I have in front of me now. How would you project a five-year plan when, using round figures, in 1954 the C.B.C. spent $31 million; in 1955, $40 million; in 1956, $49 million; in 1957, $62 million and this year an estimated $70 million. There is an increase of over 100 per cent in five years, and it is still going on.
I suggest that in the changing conditions of the present day, with the expansion of the microwave service and the other technical developments which may come-colour television for instance is something which may come in the relatively near future-together with the expansion of the service to the north, all these things depending on the general financial situation of the country, it cannot be expected that it will be practical to establish a five-year program. I invite the committee to consider the figures which I have read, which show an increase of over 100 per cent in five years. I wonder where the expenditure will be in another five years time.

Broadcasting
I am perfectly happy to leave it so a nonCanadian could get one but there is an obvious flaw in the bill as pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition. If the committee is prepared to accept it I should like to have moved an amendment striking out subclause (b) entirely and relettering subclause (c) to become (b). I believe that will meet the question raised by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. When the bill is amended further consideration could be given to providing for non-Canadians seeking a licence. This is the quickest and simplest way to deal with it at the moment.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should just like to say a word on the suggestion made by the minister. I understand he has not formally moved the motion yet. I am very sympathetic with what the minister was trying to do in this clause as I imagine the minister would expect me to be because a person who is lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence is a person who has come here, landed as an immigrant, with the intention of remaining here and becoming a citizen. When we say we do not like the idea of a foreigner having a licence to operate a station in Canada, that is a position I believe everyone in the committee would feel a proper one to take. But in a country of immigration like this it is in a way perhaps rather difficult to say that people who have every intention of leaving permanently their former country of residence and becoming citizens of this country should be denied for at least five years the opportunity of getting a licence. I do not think, in fact, this would be any great hardship because in circumstances of that sort it is always possible to make certain legal arrangements through partnerships and things of that sort so the licensee could probably be a Canadian citizen and the other person could become an employee for the time being. Some arrangement of that sort could be worked out so I doubt if any great hardship would be worked if this were taken out.
I suppose the minister has given consideration to the other effect it will have if he does this. It will make the new legislation more restrictive than the present Canadian Broadcasting Act because that act leaves it open to any British subject to have a licence. This will mean that in the future no one who is not a Canadian citizen can have a licence. I am not trying to create any difficulties for the government but am attempting to assist the government solve a genuine difficulty. The other point that was raised was also quite serious. If we were going to leave it in I had intended to suggest we add something like this-and this is just a suggestion

Broadcasting
-to the clause, that after the words "six years" and before the word "or" the following words be added: "But such licence shall automatically be revoked if the licensee having so resided for six years has not become a Canadian citizen."
It seemed to me that to give a licence to someone because he could not legally become a Canadian citizen and then to allow him to go on without becoming a Canadian citizen and retaining his licence would be something we would not want to have happen. As far as we are concerned I believe we would take the view that if the minister thinks this is the best thing to do for the time being we would have no objection to the amendment.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe it is probably the best thing to do. I have an open mind on the question. I have been so advised by the officials tonight, having in mind that we could carefully consider this when the committee meets during the next session of parliament. If it meets with the general approval of this committee I would ask my colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to move an amendment to this clause which will result in taking out subclause (b) and relettering (c) to become (b).

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move:
That section 14 be amended by deleting clause (b) and that clause (c) be relettered as clause (b).
Amendment (Mrs. Fairclough) agreed to.
Clause 14, as amended, agreed to.
Title agreed to.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: One question; the minister said that either on his estimates or before the end of this debate he might be able to give us some indication whether paragraph (6) of clause 3 precludes the present members of the C.B.C. board of governors from becoming members of the board of broadcast governors. Is he in a position to tell us that now?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.

I am advised it is not possible because one comes into operation and the other goes out of operation, and therefore you cannot be a member of both boards at the same time.

I feel I would be saving the time of the house by reading the editorial instead of-

It has been suggested by some of the newer members of the house that I should read this editorial quickly. I have a long acquaintance with, and great respect for, the editors of the Ottawa Journal and they do not write to be read quickly; they write to be read at leisure, with the full enjoyment of their sentiments and I would not wish to do less than justice, in so far as it is possible for me at all, to the sentiments expressed in this editorial.
The editorial is entitled:
C.B.C. and Parliament; Too Fast, Too Uncertain. Mr. Nowlan, as the responsible minister-

That, of course, is not quite correct. I do not mean to suggest that he is not a responsible minister, but in this context I always described the relationship of the minister and his connection with the C.B.C. as a drain pipe.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, unanimous consent was given to the reading of this editorial so that it would shut the hon. member up. Since he is going to interpolate all the way through, I would suggest that he make his speech and throw the editorial away.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
I think the minister is right, sir, and I will refrain from any interpolations. I continue with the editorial:
Mr. Nowlan, as the responsible minister, says that when the broadcasting act is passed "the C.B.C. will find itself in a stronger position than ever before". Why? Because, he says, it will be relieved of the friction-causing duty of regulation of private stations which will be taken over by the new board of broadcasting governors.
But, says Mr. Pearson, the new legislation will weaken the position of the C.B.C. and could lead to two systems of broadcasting, one private and one public, with the C.B.C. given no special position and presenting the danger that the B.B.G. might give more attention to private broadcasters than to the national system.
Mr. Nowlan speaks of the B.B.G. as "the overriding agency which is going to lay down the regulations and to enforce them". This sounds like no milk-and-water board of amiable gentlemen prepared to let the C.B.C. do pretty well as it likes. It sounds like a board of extensive power, competent to interfere with minute details of C.B.C. operations.
Mr. Pearson fears, and we think with reason, that the 15-man board of broadcast governors and the 11-man board of C.B.C. directors will get in each other's way to the detriment of the national service.
None will doubt the good intentions of the government-
This is a terrible temptation!
None will doubt the good intentions of the government or even take lightly Mr. Nowlan's contention that a fundamental problem-the allocation of authority over broadcasting-has been solved. But in spite of the minister's reassurances, the text of the bill leaves unanswered the question whether the C.B.C. is to have authority and freedom to maintain a good national service.
The time for further discussion is short. But if the legislation is passed without a full answer to that question parliament-and that means all parties-will not have done its job.
Well, sir, we have not had that answer. We on this side of the house do not want this bill to pass and it is our intention to vote against third reading.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to explain that we are going to vote for the bill for reasons we have indicated earlier. I may sum this up in essence by saying that we feel matters cannot be further delayed. We accept the assurance of
Broadcasting
the minister that a committee of the house at the next session will deal with a review of the act and have some sort of meeting or liaison with the board of broadcast governors. We support the legislation. Some of our misgivings have been allayed by the candid way in which the minister spoke and met some of our amendments suggesting changes with sympathy. We are going to be optimistic about the eventual outcome of this bill.
I want to enter, if I may, a few remarks by a Mr. Finlay MacDonald who was once general manager of the Canadian association of radio and television broadcasters. This is from an article entitled:
Will The Conservatives "Bell" the C.B.C.?
This article appeared in the Atlantic Advocate of January, 1958. The particular paragraph in this article that interests me has little or nothing to do with the bill but it indicates the hopes that we have:
It is now most interesting to observe the change in a group of men going from opposition to government. The fire of their criticism has been replaced by the studied, defensive consideration of their replies. Where before, they represented the grievances of the individual citizen, they must now be responsive to those issues of interest to the larger segments. What else would we expect?
I would say that we expect that the very best intentions which have been expressed by the minister will come to pass and that our dealings with the board of broadcast governors next session when they come before the select committee will be harmonious. I also trust that we will discover that everything has turned out for the best under this not quite the best of all possible bills.
